items.title: 2027: Opposition alliances ‘ll fail again, Fashola declares at APC Lagos rally
items.description: AHEAD of 2027 general elections, former Governor of Lagos State and former Minister of Works and Housing, Babatunde Fashola, has declared that emerging opposition coalitions will suffer the same fate as past failed alliances in Nigeria’s political history. ​Fashola made the assertion yesterday while speaking as the Chief Host at the Babatunde Raji Fashola, BRF Support Group (BRFSG) Campaign kick-off rally, held at the National Stadium in Surulere, Lagos, where he also launched a grassroots mobilisation drive aimed at building a 10,000-strong volunteer base to secure the re-election of President Bola Tinubu and the election of Lagos State Deputy Governor, Dr. Kadri Obafemi Hamzat, as the state’s next governor scheduled for January 16 and February 6, 2027, respectively. The initiative is designed to establish a volunteer-based mobilisation structure across communities, markets, streets and households ahead of the presidential and governorship elections ​ Contrasting the APC 2013 political merger with ongoing talks among rival parties, Fashola, addressing the mammoth crowd of party stalwarts, former heads of service, lawmakers, and students in Lagos, maintained that historical coalitions in 1964, 1983, and 1999 all collapsed without winning the presidency. He dismissed critics who once labeled the APC’s founding blocs as “strange bedfellows,” noting that while the ruling party has consolidated, the opposition has fragmented. ​ “This APC was and remains the only merger that has happened in the history of Nigeria’s political parliament. All of the alliances you have seen on the horizon now will fail too, with your votes,” Fashola told the gathering.Those who see conflict in their party and run away, don’t trust them. They will leave you when things are tough.They don’t stand for anything; they will fall for everything,” he warned. ​​“The intention is to achieve a volunteer party base of 10,000 people, working from now all through to election day, knocking doors, carrying the message of our party, explaining what our party has done, explaining what the candidates have done, explaining what the government has done,” Fashola stated. ​ ​Highlighting the APC’s track record in governance, Fashola pointed to major infrastructure milestones, including: the Lekki Deep Sea Port, the Second Niger Bridge, the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway, and the Lagos-Ibadan Railway, as proof of the party’s commitment to long-term economic growth over short-term savings. Hamzat rallies Lagos APC supporters ​The governorship candidate, Hamzat, on his address launched a spirited defence of the ruling party’s governance record, contrasting the APC’s development “blueprint” against what he described as the opposition’s “manifesto of grievances.” ​Addressing the gathering, Hamzat urged APC canvassers to take a bold, fact-based message to voters ahead of the 2027 general elections. He emphasized that the upcoming polls are consequential for both Lagos State and Nigeria’s ongoing economic reforms. ​ Taking a swipe at rival political parties, Hamzat accused opposition figures of peddling falsehoods and backtracking on policies they once championed, specifically referencing the removal of the fuel subsidy. Equipping party faithful for door-to-door campaigns, Hamzat outlined key achievements of the Babajide Sanwo-Olu administration and President Tinubu’s federal government, noting that Lagos has domesticated the Electricity Act signed by President Tinubu, enabling the state to participate in power generation, transmission, and distribution. ​Expressing concern over low voter turnout in previous cycles, Hamzat challenged residents to match the state’s high voter registration numbers at the ballot box. The post 2027: Opposition alliances ‘ll fail again, Fashola declares at APC Lagos rally appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Carnet noir à New York : La communauté burkinabè sous le choc après le rappel à Dieu de Anne Kontiebo
items.description: La communauté des ressortissants burkinabè aux États-Unis est endeuillée par une triste disparition. Par l'intermédiaire d'un communiqué officiel rendu public ce jeudi 26 novembre 2026, l’Association des Burkinabè de New-York (ABNY) a annoncé le décès de leur compatriote, Mlle Anne Kontiebo, survenu la veille à l’hôpital NYU Langone. Alors que le programme des obsèques reste à préciser, l'organisation communautaire a rapidement exprimé ses condoléances à la famille et amorcé l'élan de solidarité. L'émotion est vive au sein de la diaspora burkinabè de la côte Est américaine. Dans un communiqué nécrologique diffusé le jeudi 26 novembre 2026, l’Association des Burkinabè de New-York (ABNY) a fait part de la disparition de Mlle Anne Kontiebo. Selon les précisions fournies par l'organisation, la défunte s’est éteinte le mercredi 25 novembre 2026 à 3 heures du matin, au sein de l’établissement hospitalier NYU Langone. Face à ce drame, la solidarité communautaire s'est immédiatement manifestée. L’ABNY a adressé ses condoléances les plus attristées aux proches et à la famille de la disparue, leur garantissant le soutien moral et les prières de l'ensemble des compatriotes vivants dans la région new-yorkaise en ces heures particulièrement difficiles. L'association indique rester dans l'attente de l'établissement du programme des obsèques pour accompagner dignement la défunte vers sa dernière demeure. Pour coordonner l'assistance et informer les membres de la diaspora, des contacts ont été mis à disposition. Les ressortissants souhaitant obtenir de plus amples informations ou manifester leur soutien peuvent joindre les responsables désignés par l'ABNY, à savoir M. Sambo au +1 (646) 510-3347 ainsi que M. J-B au +1 (917) 306-5738. L'association a conclu sa communication en invoquant le repos de l'âme de la défunte. L’article Carnet noir à New York : La communauté burkinabè sous le choc après le rappel à Dieu de Anne Kontiebo est apparu en premier sur NetAfrique.net .

items.title: Stay away from our state, Imo APC tells Wike
items.description: The All Progressives Congress, APC, in Imo State, has declared that the state is not available for political manipulation or interference by the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Nyesom Wike. Read Also: ‘I’m done with Rivers, FCT; give me Imo, Kwara to deliver’ – Wike tells Tinubu It vowed to resist any attempt to import what it described as his controversial political tactics into the state ahead of the 2027 general elections. The party made its position known in a statement yesterday by its State Publicity Secretary, Onwuasoanya Jones in reaction to alleged Wike’s recent claim that he had concluded arrangements to secure electoral victories for President Bola Tinubu and the APC in the forthcoming elections. Wike was also reported to have offered to undertake additional political assignments for the President, including delivering other states for the APC. Reacting, the Imo APC dismissed the minister’s claims, contending that he should not assume that his political activities could determine the electoral fortunes of the party in different states. The statement particularly faulted Wike for reportedly suggesting that Imo State and another APC-controlled state had political problems requiring his intervention. “We would have ignored the politically displaced errand boy, like we always do, but for the fact that we deem this particular statement of his a direct affront on the President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and the electoral integrity of our dear party, the APC,” the statement declared. The party accused the FCT minister of attempting to portray President Tinubu as politically dependent on individuals outside the APC to secure electoral victories, insisting that the party enjoys its own grassroots support and political structure. It also faulted Wike’s reported assertion that he had already secured victory for the APC in the FCT and Rivers State, describing such declarations, made weeks before the elections, as disrespectful to democratic principles and the electorate. According to the statement, “our party, the All Progressives Congress, has immense regard for the Nigerian people and would not encourage actions and utterances that tend to cast the Nigerian electorate as irrelevant in the determination of their political future.” The Imo APC further accused Wike of taking advantage of the party’s political goodwill to sustain his relevance while allegedly making disparaging remarks about some of its leaders. It challenged the minister to demonstrate his political influence by campaigning for his own party, the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), rather than making claims about delivering APC victories. On the political situation in Imo State, the party maintained that its activities were progressing without difficulty and expressed confidence in its preparations for the 2027 elections. It said its mobilisation efforts across the state were ongoing, adding that it expected Imo voters to participate in the forthcoming elections scheduled for January 16 and February 6, 2027, as stated in the release. The statement also alleged that Wike had deployed political associates and emissaries to Imo State with financial inducements in an attempt to create divisions within the APC. However, the party did not provide specific details or independent evidence to substantiate the allegation. Describing the alleged moves as an attempt to introduce godfatherism, political intimidation and electoral manipulation into the state, the APC said it had warned those reportedly involved against such activities. items.title: World: Waiting to tackle HIV in the Pacific could double the cost and prevent fewer infections
items.description: Countries: World, Fiji, Papua New Guinea Source: Australian National University Caroline van Gemert Anna Bowring Jason Mitchell Donald Wilson Across the Pacific, communities are confronting growing human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) outbreaks at a time when health budgets are constrained and international development assistance is increasingly uncertain . Fiji has one of the fastest-growing HIV epidemics globally, with new infections rising approximately twelvefold between 2010 and 2025 . Papua New Guinea has declared a national HIV crisis , while several other Pacific Island countries and territories are now reporting early warning signs of increased transmission. When responding to an HIV outbreak, when to invest, how much to invest and what to invest in all shape outcomes. The challenge is not only to secure enough funding, but to make sure it reaches the right people and arrives early enough to change the course of an outbreak. To examine these trade-offs, we used Optima HIV , a mathematical and economic modelling tool that has been applied around the world to identify how HIV resources can be allocated to minimise new infections and HIV-related deaths. We modelled a hypothetical Pacific Island country of 100,000 people with an emerging HIV outbreak, using regional epidemiological, behavioural, service and cost data. We compared current approaches with an optimised response: treatment and adherence support for people already diagnosed, plus targeted prevention and testing for key populations . Key populations are the groups most affected by HIV, such as men who have sex with men and people who inject drugs, and they often have limited access to services. We tested this response across several outbreak profiles, starting in either 2027 or 2030. Four findings emerged: act early, prioritise treatment and adherence support for people already diagnosed, focus prevention and testing on key populations and expect costs to rise before they fall. First, acting early costs less and prevents more infections. Doubling existing annual HIV investment from 2027 (from about USD32,700 to USD65,500 per 100,000 population per year) and optimising the response was projected to avert more than 90% of new infections by 2040, compared with continuing current approaches. Delaying this response until 2030 would cost on average USD132,500 per 100,000 population per year to achieve a similar result — about twice the annual cost of investing from 2027 — yet would avert fewer infections (86%). The difference in effectiveness and cost between an early and a delayed response comes down to how HIV spreads. Transmission compounds over time, so an infection prevented today also prevents infections further along the chain. As an outbreak accelerates, a much larger investment is needed just to regain lost ground. Second, maximising treatment engagement and outcomes among people who are diagnosed is the priority. In the model, scaling up treatment, engagement in care and adherence support did the most to increase viral suppression and prevent onward transmission. Fiji shows why this matters: only 56% of reported people living with HIV were receiving antiretroviral treatment at the end of 2025, and only 15% of those on treatment had documented viral suppression, meaning the virus had been reduced to a level that prevents onward transmission . Coverage across all people estimated to be living with HIV in Fiji, including those not yet diagnosed, is lower still: Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS puts it at about 22% . Third, prevention and testing should focus first on key populations. Testing and prevention services designed for these groups had a bigger impact than generalised testing and condom programs, because this is where the virus spreads. Fourth, spending rises first, then falls. Reported diagnoses reveal only part of an outbreak. In our model, around 31% of people living with HIV were diagnosed in 2025, so expanded testing finds many more people who need treatment and adherence support, and that raises costs in the short term. But as future infections are prevented, those projected needs decline. Within about a decade, an optimised response was projected to need fewer treatment and adherence resources than continuing with current approaches. Together, the findings show countries do not need to wait to deliver a perfect HIV response. Where resources are limited, starting with the interventions most likely to interrupt transmission, then expanding as resources and capacity grow, is more effective than delaying action. This is not an argument for less HIV funding in the Pacific. It is an argument for targeted investment. Additional domestic and development-partner investment is critical. The finding is that the timing of investment can be just as consequential as its size. These findings are not a prescription for any individual Pacific country. Local epidemiology, service costs, practical constraints and equity priorities must shape how governments invest. Country-specific Optima models can be built using national epidemiological and program data, with local priorities in mind, and we would welcome the chance to work with ministries and partners to do so. Which key populations to reach first depends on the outbreak, and in many Pacific countries it is not yet clear what is driving the rise in infections or which populations are affected. Transmission patterns differ between countries and change over time, so we modelled different outbreak profiles, including varying sexual and injecting drug-use-related risks. Without a clear picture of who is most affected, governments cannot be sure where to direct scarce resources. That is why better surveillance data matters: timely local data on who is being infected, and whether they are reaching care, is what allows countries to target their response and adjust it as the outbreak changes. For governments and development partners, the priority should be to secure effective funding before transmission accelerates, to protect services that reach key populations, to support people to start and stay on treatment and to ensure programs can adapt to local needs. Sustained investment, strong surveillance, better case monitoring and sound epidemiological data are crucial to directing resources as outbreak patterns change. Pacific governments have already signalled where they want to go. At the 17th Pacific Heads of Health meeting in Rarotonga in August 2026, heads of health accepted two recommendations. The first is that every Pacific Island country and territory develop or strengthen a national HIV preparedness and response plan within 12 months, including functional HIV surveillance and real-time early-warning indicators. The second is that a Pacific HIV Regional Support Mechanism be established within 18 months. These measures provide a foundation for the kind of early, targeted and sustained investment supported by our modelling. The commitments have been agreed. What they need now is resourcing. HIV transmission does not pause while budgets are negotiated. The cost of waiting is paid twice: in preventable infections today, and in the greater resources needed to control outbreaks tomorrow. The authors would like to acknowledge the contributions of Burnet Head of Modelling and Biostatistics, Associate Professor Nick Scott, and Burnet Head of Public Health, Professor Mark Stoové, for their modelling and expertise underpinning this post.

items.title: Community attacked 24 times by bandits wants exit from Kaduna
items.description: For the people of Kurmin Wali community in Afogo Ward, Kajuru Local Government Area of Kaduna State, incessant attacks by bandits have made them start thinking of relocating to where they could find peace. The simple desire to sleep peacefully in their homes has become an increasingly distant dream. For years, residents have lived under the agony of armed attacks, abductions and ransom demands, with the community reportedly attacked by bandits 24 times. As a result, many families are not only battling the fear of being kidnapped but also hunger, poverty and the emotional burden of having their loved ones in captivity. Some residents say they have reached the end of their endurance and are contemplating leaving their ancestral homes in search of safety elsewhere. “We are leaving. We have sold our food to pay ransom. We are hungry and traumatised,” a resident lamented, describing the devastating consequences of repeated attacks on the farming community. The latest attack occurred on Sunday, November 15, when armed men invaded the community and abducted 12 residents, renewing fears among villagers that another round of suffering had begun. For the people of Kurmin Wali, however, the incident was not just another attack. It was the 24th time, according to residents, that the community had suffered attacks and abductions by armed criminals. The repeated incidents have left families emotionally drained, with some struggling to raise money for the release of relatives while others have been forced to sell food and other possessions to meet ransom demands. For a community largely dependent on subsistence farming, the situation has become particularly unbearable. The people who should be preparing their farms and harvesting food to feed their families are instead preoccupied with the desperate search for money to secure the freedom of their loved ones. The Village Head, Isiaku Danazumi, said the community was exhausted by the persistent attacks and appealed to Governor Uba Sani to fulfil his earlier promise to facilitate the establishment of a military base in the area. “They have attacked and kidnapped our people 24 times. Each time they come, the community is thrown into fear and trauma. Even me, I am not feeling well as we speak,” he said. The traditional ruler said the community had endured so much that residents were beginning to question how much longer they could continue living under such circumstances. “We are tired. We cannot continue like this. Where can we go again? How can we abandon our ancestral home because of this?” he asked. Beyond the physical danger, the repeated attacks have inflicted deep psychological wounds on the villagers, who live with the uncertainty of whether their relatives will return home safely or whether another invasion will occur. Danazumi said residents had identified a recurring route allegedly used by the attackers, particularly the forest corridor linking Maro and Rijana. According to him, the attackers have repeatedly approached the community through Maro, with residents suspecting that the criminals operate from the Rijana axis through adjoining forests. He recalled that Governor Uba Sani had promised to facilitate the establishment of a military base in the area following the mass abduction of worshippers during the Easter period earlier this year. “We are making a strong appeal to our Governor, Uba Sani, to speed up the military base he promised us earlier in the year when several of our people were abducted during the Easter celebration,” the village head pleaded. He described the proposed military base as an urgent necessity, saying the community could no longer cope with the financial and emotional consequences of repeated ransom payments. “A military base around here is the only solution for now. We are tired of paying ransom. We are just an agrarian community that farms with hoes and cutlasses,” he said. The village head further disclosed that some residents were still being held captive despite efforts by their families and the community to raise money for their release. “We have our people in their custody. We have raised ransom, and up till now, they have not freed them,” he added. The plight of Kurmin Wali is part of the wider security challenges confronting rural communities, particularly settlements located close to forest corridors suspected to be used by armed groups. Rijana, along the Kaduna-Abuja Expressway in Kachia Local Government Area, has repeatedly featured in accounts of kidnapping incidents in the state. In January 2026, following the abduction of 177 worshippers from churches in Kurmin Wali, Governor Uba Sani identified Rijana as a major security concern and called for the establishment of a military base close to the affected community. In May 2026, eight farmers abducted near Kankomi village were reportedly released from a bandits’ camp in Rijana Forest after spending weeks in captivity. For the people of Kurmin Wali, however, the statistics of attacks, abductions and ransom payments represent something much more painful than security figures. They represent families separated from loved ones, farmers deprived of their livelihoods, children growing up in fear and households forced to sell the food meant to sustain them. As another painful chapter unfolds following the November 15 attack, the residents are left with a desperate question: how long must they continue to live this way before they can sleep peacefully in their own homes? For a people whose lives revolve around farming, family and their ancestral land, leaving may become the only option they believe is left. But for now, they are appealing for protection before fear and hunger finally drive them away. items.title: Security chiefs hail IGP Disu for suspending declaration of Obaigbena, others wanted
items.description: By Emma Nnadozie THE police order suspending the wanted declaration on Arise TV owner, Mr. Nduka Obaigbena and seven others over alleged assassination attempt by Assistant Inspector-General of Police, Olohundare Jimoh, has elicited reactions from some security chiefs in the country, who said that the wanted declaration was done without due process. One of the security chiefs who spoke with Vanguard, said: “It was misappropriate and procedurally flawed” and showered encomiums on the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, for his quick response by suspending the wanted declaration The Assistant Inspector-General of Police, Zone 2, Onikan, Lagos, Olohundare Jimoh, last Tuesday, declared Chairman of Arise News and This Day Media Group, Chief Nduka Obaigbena, Managing Director of Nestoil, Dr. Ernest Azudialu-Obiejesi, and seven others wanted over an alleged threat to the life of First Bank Managing Director, Olusegun Alebiosu in a crowed press conference in Lagos. He said the declaration followed an investigation into the delivery of a parcel containing two rounds of 7.62mm live ammunition to Alebiosu’s residence in Lagos. However, in a swift reaction two days later, the IGP, through the Force Public Relations Officer, FPRO, Ani Iniedu suspended the wanted declaration against the suspects and stated that the case has been transferred to the Force Intelligence Department, FID, Abuja, for a thorough and impartial investigation. He also directed the nine individuals to report to the FID, at the Force headquarters , Abuja, between November 26 and 30, 2026. In his reaction, the Director-General of the Institute of Security, Nigeria at the University of Lagos, Mr. Adebayo Akinade, said that the Zone 2 declaration was “misappropriate and procedurally flawed. The IGP’s suspension and transfer to Force Intelligence Department was correct, strategic and has restored public confidence.” Former Director with the Department of State Service, DSS, and currently a security consultant, Mr. Mike Ejiofor, said: “The IGP has the superior order on such matters. When a subordinate makes a mistake, the IGP is in a position to correct it. So, I do not see any conflict in the matter.” In his response the Chairman/Chief Executive Officer of Perfect Security Services Limited, Dr. Patrick Uwagbale saw the incident as “part of a system that is not in order. A good society will do something according to the rules. Even if the allegation is true or not, it is unheard of that someone as IGP would be on seat and a subordinate had the audacity to take such a decision on such a high profile incident without authorisation from the IGP who ordinarily should have the last say on such a matter. This type of behaviour clearly shows that our system is not healthy. “Something is wrong somewhere. There is a gap somewhere. I wholly support the decision of the IGP to suspend the declaration by his subordinate.” Recall also that The Chairman of This Day Newspapers and Arise, Nduka Obaigbena also denied that he has been declared wanted by the Nigeria Police Force, following a petition by the bank Chief. In a statement by his office in Ikoyi, Lagos, he described the reports as a “desperate smear campaign,” insisting that neither the police nor any other law enforcement agency had invited him for questioning. items.title: Four injured as tanker, medicine truck and passenger vehicle crash on Fumesua-Ejisu Road
items.description: Four people have been injured in a three-vehicle collision involving a fuel tanker, a truck carrying medicines for Shalom Pharmacy Limited and a passenger Ford vehicle on the Fumesua-Ejisu Road in the Ashanti Region. The crash, which occurred at about 2:30 p.m. on Thursday, November 26, brought traffic on the busy road to a near standstill, leaving motorists caught in long queues. The injured victims, who reportedly suffered varying degrees of injuries, were conveyed to the KNUST Hospital for treatment. Personnel of the Ghana National Fire Service and the Ghana Police Service responded to the scene to assist with the emergency and manage the aftermath of the collision. The accident disrupted movement along the Fumesua-Ejisu stretch, with drivers and passengers facing hours of delays as emergency crews attended to the incident. The cause of the crash had not been established at the time of filing this report. There was also no immediate information on the extent of damage to the three vehicles.

items.title: 2027 Elections: INEC raises alarm, warns violence may hurt polls
items.description: By Ikechukwu Nnochiri and Omeiza Ajayi ABUJA — Chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, Prof. Joash Amupitan, yesterday, warned that the raging waves of political violence could harm the 2027 general elections. Listing Lagos, Edo, Ekiti, Enugu, Ebonyi, Delta, Cross River, Oyo and Benue as states where incidents of political violence had been recorded, he warned political parties and their supporters against violence, intimidation and the use of thugs, saying such activities could discourage voter participation and undermine the credibility of the 2027 elections. He also cautioned political parties against signing peace accords in Abuja while allegedly sponsoring violence in states, insisting that no political ambition was worth the blood of Nigerians. According to him, attacks have targeted campaign convoys, town hall meetings, party offices and supporters, while INEC officials, staff and ad hoc personnel have also suffered harassment, intimidation and physical attacks by supporters and agents of political parties, both within Nigeria and abroad. It also said it was working with closely with the Nigeria Police Force and allied security agencies to prosecute electoral offenders. The warning came as INEC and security agencies met in Abuja to strengthen election security ahead of the 2027 polls. This came as the Federal Government assured voters, politicians, electoral officials and political parties of protection before, during and after the elections. Speaking at a Strategic Election Security Conference jointly convened by INEC and the Office of the National Security Adviser, ONSA, Amupitan said Nigeria had witnessed a disturbing escalation in political intolerance, inflammatory rhetoric and coordinated attacks since the commencement of campaigns in August 2026. Addressing political parties, he said: “Signing peace accords in Abuja while tolerating or financing thuggery in the states is a contradiction our democracy can no longer afford.” He warned that INEC would not succumb to threats or intimidation. “We will neither be intimidated nor blackmailed into compromising our neutrality, and every attack on INEC personnel, facilities, or materials will be met with the full weight of the law,” INEC chairman said. Amupitan said responsibility for electoral violence extended beyond those directly involved in attacks, stressing that political party leaders must be held accountable for the conduct of their candidates and supporters. He said: “Accountability does not end with the foot soldiers who throw stones or wield weapons,” adding that “party leadership bears moral and political responsibility for the conduct of its candidates, campaign councils, and youth wings”. Violence may suppress voter turnout The INEC chairman identified three major consequences of political violence for the electoral process, including voter suppression, threats to the safety of electoral personnel and the possibility of post-election violence. On voter suppression, he said: “When bullets replace ballots and rallies end in bloodshed, ordinary citizens stay home, effectively disenfranchising millions of peaceful Nigerians.” He said the second concern was the safety of more than 1.41 million ad hoc personnel, most of them National Youth Service Corps, NYSC, members, to be deployed across 177,299 polling units. “No parent or institution will willingly deploy young Nigerians into environments where political thugs operate with impunity,” he said. On the third consequence, Amupitan warned that violence before elections could create an atmosphere of hostility and rejection after the announcement of results. “Pre-election violence conditions the political climate for post-election rejection,” he said, warning that collation centres could become flashpoints. He said the need to get elections right in Nigeria is because of the regional implications. The country accounts for more than half of West Africa’s population. A peaceful election, he said, would serve as “the primary anchor of regional stability and constitutional order”. Faults arrest provision Turning to enforcement, Amupitan expressed concern over a provision in the Regulations and Guidelines for the Conduct of Elections, 2026, which allows security agents to arrest electoral offenders only on the instruction of presiding officers or other INEC officials. “This dichotomy has hampered the efficiency of the law enforcement agents to arrest and investigate electoral offenders,” he said. He noted that the same regulations empowered security agencies to prevent violence and activities capable of disrupting elections. The chairman called for the issue to be addressed through a code of conduct and a proposed legal framework for the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security, ICCES. He said the Electoral Act 2026 had increased penalties for electoral offences to fines of up to N5 million or 12 months’ imprisonment for individuals, while political parties could face fines of up to N10 million for first breaches. Amupitan added that Section 148 of the Act empowered INEC legal officers and appointed counsel to prosecute electoral offenders directly once case files were transmitted by the police and other relevant agencies. “INEC is fully prepared to discharge its prosecutorial mandate, and our legal teams are ready to review case files from recent violent incidents across the federation,” he said. Amupitan added: “When political actors see prominent sponsors and foot soldiers swiftly arrested, arraigned, and convicted under the 2026 Act, the incentive for violent campaigns will evaporate.” Over 100m verified voters Providing an update on preparations for the elections at the commission’s meeting with Resident Electoral Commissioners, RECs, from the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory, FCT, Amupitan said INEC was managing a verified voter register of more than 100 million. He said the commission had removed more than 1.6 million invalid, duplicated and deceased records from its supplementary voters’ register following the application of an Automated Biometric Identification System, ABIS, and a statutory claims and objections audit. The exercise reduced the earlier figure of 103 million registered voters to more than 100 million verified records. Amupitan also disclosed that INEC had selected 17,676 polling units for its Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, BVAS, mock accreditation and result upload exercise scheduled for Saturday, November 28, 2026, ahead of the 2027 general elections. He urged security commanders to treat the exercise as a full-scale rehearsal for the elections. The INEC chairman said the presidential and National Assembly elections would hold on Saturday, January 16, 2027, while governorship and state Houses of Assembly elections would take place on Saturday, February 6, 2027. FG assures voters, politicians of protection Meanwhile, the National Security Adviser, NSA, Mallam Nuhu Ribadu, assured Nigerians that the Federal Government and security agencies would protect voters, politicians, electoral officials and political parties before, during and after the elections. Ribadu, who spoke at the conference, said the administration of President Bola Tinubu was committed to providing the security required for peaceful, transparent and credible elections. “The duty of government and the security agencies is to protect voters, electoral officials and the wider population before, during and after the election. We will protect you. We will protect the voters. We will protect politicians. And even after the election, we will make sure there is no violence,” he declared. He pledged that security agencies would operate impartially and in accordance with the law. “Security agencies will discharge their responsibilities impartially and in accordance with the law,” he said. Ribadu said constitutional independence must be respected, particularly with a professor of law heading INEC. He also identified social media misinformation as a major threat to electoral security, warning that false narratives could trigger violence. “Social media is a big problem. It creates false narratives and misinformation, causing problems among people. One individual, sitting somewhere in a village, could say something that triggers trouble,” he said. The NSA also cautioned politicians against desperate actions in their quest for political power. “Sometimes they become desperate. There is almost nothing they may not do,” he said. Earlier, the Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu, called for improved collaboration, intelligence sharing and coordinated security operations among relevant agencies to address potential threats to the electoral process. The meeting was attended by the NSA, the IGP, Director-General of the State Security Service, Oluwatosin Ajayi, and other security and electoral officials. We’re working with security agencies to prosecute offenders – INEC Meanwhile, Amupitan, SAN, who spoke at the opening session of the 2026 Annual Conference of the National Association of Judiciary Correspondents, NAJUC, in Abuja, said the Commission would initiate action against identified offenders upon receipt of investigative case files from the relevant security agencies. In a goodwill message by his Chief Press Secretary, CPS, Mr. Adedayo Oketola, the INEC Chairman insisted that the integrity of Nigeria’s democratic process depends on seamless institutional synergy between those who conduct elections and those who adjudicate electoral disputes. “When the polling unit produces credible records and the tribunal applies the law with dispatch and consistency, public trust in both the ballot and the verdict is reinforced. “Public confidence in democracy erodes whenever citizens perceive that elections are won in the courtroom rather than at the polling unit — or, conversely, when judicial processes are weaponised through frivolous pre-election and post-election litigation. “Equally damaging is the distortion of judicial pronouncements in public discourse, where nuanced rulings are stripped of legal context and weaponised to inflame political tension. “We need an electoral commission that conducts transparent, verifiable polls; political parties that respect internal democracy and the rule of law; courts that dispense predictable, substantial justice; and a judiciary press corps committed to precision and fairness. “For INEC, the best way to ease the litigation burden on our courts ahead of the Presidential and National Assembly elections on January 16, 2027, and the governorship and state Houses of Assembly polls on February 6, 2027, starting with our nationwide mock accreditation and result transmission exercise this November 28, 2026, is to eliminate administrative ambiguity at the source.” Meanwhile, in his presentation, the immediate past President of the Nigerian Bar Association, NBA, Mr. Afam Osigwe, SAN, who was the lead speaker at the conference, said he was worried that moneybags were hijacking elections in the country. “The type of electoral process we have is making it difficult for honest persons to contest elections. Moneybags are hijacking the elections. “Wrong persons who have no business seeking leadership positions are the ones fighting for elective offices, and it should not be that way,” Osigwe stated. He argued that courts should not be involved in determining who represents a political party at an election. The NBA President, Mrs. Oyinkansola Badejo-Okusanya, SAN, who was represented by Dr. Prince Azubuike, said electoral credibility depends not only on free, fair and transparent elections but also on the integrity of the judicial processes through which disputes are determined. items.title: Environnement : les médias culturels mobilisés pour sensibiliser aux défis écologiques
items.description: La sensibilisation aux changements climatiques et à la préservation des ressources naturelles était au cœur d’une rencontre organisée mercredi à Casablanca, dans le cadre de la quatrième édition du Salon international du livre enfant et jeunesse (SILEJ). Les échanges ont porté sur la contribution des contenus culturels, scientifiques et patrimoniaux à la diffusion d’une conscience environnementale auprès du grand public. La rencontre a notamment permis de présenter plusieurs émissions consacrées aux questions écologiques, dont « Ecologica », « Al Baheth » et « Matahif Wa Athar », diffusées par la chaîne Athaqafia de la Société nationale de radiodiffusion et de télévision (SNRT). Les intervenants ont mis en avant différentes approches, allant du traitement de problématiques quotidiennes comme la désertification et la raréfaction de l’eau à la vulgarisation des recherches sur le stress hydrique et les énergies renouvelables. Les échanges ont également porté sur le rôle du patrimoine dans la sensibilisation des jeunes générations, notamment à travers les collections muséales qui témoignent de la biodiversité autrefois présente au Maroc et des transformations de l’environnement naturel. Prenant part à cette rencontre, organisée dans le cadre du programme du stand institutionnel de la SNRT, Zouhour Himmich, directrice d’Athaqafia, a souligné que les médias culturels ont un rôle à jouer dans la construction d’une conscience collective autour des enjeux environnementaux. Les intervenants ont aussi rappelé l’importance de rapprocher ces sujets du quotidien des citoyens, en faisant le lien entre les défis écologiques, les initiatives nationales et les contributions de la recherche scientifique. Pour rappel, le Salon international du livre enfant et jeunesse est organisé pour sa 4è édition, du 21 au 29 novembre à Casablanca, sous le thème « Littérature et environnement : les récits de la nature ». items.title: 2027: Why North will vote for Tinubu — Uba Sani
items.description: By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo Kaduna State Governor, Uba Sani, has said the North has sufficient reasons to vote for President Bola Tinubu in the January 16, 2027 presidential election, citing what he described as unprecedented infrastructure development and investments in education and other sectors under the administration. Sani said presidential candidates should campaign based on their records in public office rather than make fresh promises, insisting that northern voters would assess what each of them had done for the region before seeking its support. The governor spoke at a programme organised by Arewa Think Tank, a pro-northern political organisation, which endorsed Tinubu and Sani for re-election in 2027. He said all leading presidential candidates had held public offices in the past and should be prepared to account for their contributions to the North. According to him, the era of campaigning with promises is over, as voters are now interested in evaluating the performance of candidates. Sani argued that the North had witnessed significant development in the last three and a half years under Tinubu, particularly in road infrastructure. He disclosed that the President had approved N600 billion for the Abuja-Kaduna-Kano highway, which he said had previously been abandoned, adding that the project would soon be completed. The governor also listed several federal road projects across the three geopolitical zones in the North. “The Federal Government has embarked on constructing 1,300 kilometres of road projects in the North-West, 1,400 kilometres of roads in the North-East and 1,200 kilometres of roads in the North-Central. Put together, this is unprecedented in Northern Nigeria,” he said. Giving a breakdown of completed projects, Sani said 348 kilometres of roads had been completed in the North-West, almost 400 kilometres in the North-East and about 355 kilometres in the North-Central. He added that other projects were at various stages of completion, ranging from 60 to 80 per cent. “How can anyone tell us not to vote for a man like that?” he asked. On education, the governor said Tinubu’s establishment of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND) had improved access to tertiary education, particularly for students from disadvantaged backgrounds. He disclosed that 63 per cent of beneficiaries of the student loan scheme were from Northern Nigeria. Sani also said about 70 per cent of beneficiaries of the Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) programme were from the North, describing the initiative as an opportunity to equip young people with practical and employable skills. “President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has done a lot for us, and we will come out on 16th January 2027 to repay him with our votes in Northern Nigeria,” he said. The governor urged northern political leaders to begin developing a blueprint for the region ahead of 2031, when he said power would return to the North. He also expressed confidence in Tinubu’s electoral prospects in Kaduna State, predicting that the President would secure 80 per cent of the votes in the state. “No presidential candidate will even have 25 per cent by the grace of God in Kaduna State, apart from President Bola Ahmed Tinubu. We are giving Asiwaju 80 per cent; the rest can share the remaining 20 per cent,” he said. Explaining his support for Tinubu, Sani said the President’s interventions had contributed to developments in Kaduna State’s health, education, agriculture and transport sectors. He cited the ongoing N178 billion Mando-Birnin Gwari road project and the Zaria-Soba-Pambegua road projects as examples of federal government interventions in the state. He also listed the proposed Kaduna Light Rail Project and disclosed that the groundbreaking ceremony for the Jema’a-Kwoi road project would take place the following week. Sani further noted that Kaduna State had benefited from federal appointments, pointing out that the Minister of Defence, the Minister of Environment and the Chairman of the National Sports Commission were from the state. The post 2027: Why North will vote for Tinubu — Uba Sani appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Government pays GH¢12.9bn to DDEP bondholders ahead of 2027 maturity
items.description: The government has paid GH¢12.89 billion to investors who accepted its offer to cash out of bonds due in February 2027, bringing forward the settlement of nearly half of the outstanding securities by several months. The first phase of the voluntary buyback covered GH¢12.6 billion in bond principal, while a further GH¢289 million was paid as accrued interest. Announcing the transaction in Parliament on Thursday, November 26, Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson said the settlement was completed at 11:15 a.m., ahead of the scheduled noon deadline. The payment, funded from the Cedi Sinking Fund, represents 44.1 per cent of the February 2027 Domestic Debt Exchange Programme (DDEP) bonds targeted under the offer. Dr Forson said the government had deliberately arranged the early repayment to demonstrate its ability and willingness to meet its obligations, while helping restore confidence in the domestic bond market. “This is how you rebuild confidence. We set the money aside, we made the offer, and we paid ahead of time,” he said. The Finance Minister said the first round of the offer opened on Monday and closed on Wednesday, with the settlement made the following day. The government is expected to give investors who did not participate another opportunity to exit their holdings. Dr Forson said the voluntary buyback would be reopened in two weeks. The transaction is part of a wider effort to manage the debt obligations arising from the restructuring of Ghana’s domestic debt in 2023. The scale of the repayments ahead is substantial. The 2027 Budget presented by Dr Forson indicates that DDEP bonds worth GH¢40.1 billion will mature in February next year, comprising GH¢29 billion in principal and GH¢11.1 billion in interest. A further GH¢12.5 billion is scheduled to fall due in August, bringing the combined obligations for the two months to about GH¢52.6 billion. The Minister had earlier disclosed that the Cedi Sinking Fund held GH¢29 billion as of November 11, an amount he said was sufficient to cover the principal component of the February maturity. Dr Forson also told Parliament that the government had made payments exceeding GH¢46.5 billion towards domestic debt obligations inherited from the previous administration. That included GH¢5.14 billion paid to investors who did not take part in the DDEP. The early settlement is intended to reduce the amount of February 2027 bonds left outstanding, although the government will still have to meet the remaining principal and interest obligations when they fall due. For bondholders who accepted the offer, the transaction provides access to their money before the original maturity date. For the government, it represents another step in its debt-management programme, with the next round expected to accommodate investors who have yet to tender their securities.

items.title: FIFM : À Marrakech, le cinéma se vit aussi dans les regards du public
items.description: Depuis le 20 novembre, Marrakech vit au rythme de la 23e édition du Festival international du film de Marrakech. Projections, rencontres, hommages et découvertes rythment les journées et les soirées de la cité ocre. Mais derrière les stars, les réalisateurs et les tapis rouges, un autre acteur occupe une place essentielle dans cette grande fête du septième art : le public. À travers les images, les spectateurs racontent à leur manière l’atmosphère particulière d’un festival où le cinéma se partage autant qu’il se regarde. À Marrakech, il suffit de se rapprocher d’une salle de projection ou des différents espaces du Festival international du film de Marrakech pour mesurer l’effervescence qui accompagne cette 23e édition. Depuis plusieurs jours, la ville accueille cinéphiles, professionnels, artistes et curieux venus découvrir des œuvres venues du Maroc et du monde entier. Dans cette agitation permanente, les visages des spectateurs racontent une autre histoire du festival. Celle de l’attente avant une projection, de la concentration pendant un film, des discussions à la sortie d’une séance ou encore de cette curiosité qui pousse à découvrir une œuvre inconnue. Mounir Mehimdate Marrakech, neuf jours au rythme du septième art Pour sa 23e édition, le FIFM continue de faire de Marrakech un point de rencontre entre différentes cinématographies et différentes générations d’artistes. La compétition officielle côtoie les sections consacrées aux découvertes, les premières, les rencontres avec les cinéastes et les grands hommages qui ponctuent le festival. Cette édition a notamment été marquée par la présence de Marion Cotillard à la tête du jury, mais aussi par les hommages rendus à de grandes figures du cinéma international et marocain, parmi lesquelles Jeff Goldblum, John Turturro ou encore Younès Mégri. Autour de ces personnalités, le festival donne également une place importante aux réalisateurs et aux nouvelles voix du cinéma. Des films venus de différents horizons sont présentés au public, avec cette volonté de faire de Marrakech un espace de découverte et de dialogue entre les cultures. Mounir Mehimdate Quand les spectateurs deviennent les visages du festival Pourtant, un festival de cinéma ne se résume jamais aux personnalités qui foulent son tapis rouge. Il existe aussi dans les salles, dans les files d’attente, dans les échanges entre spectateurs et dans les réactions qui suivent une projection. Le public est celui qui reçoit les films, les interprète, les questionne et leur donne parfois une seconde vie à travers les discussions. Un regard attentif, un sourire, une expression de surprise ou simplement une concentration silencieuse peuvent en dire autant sur l’expérience du FIFM qu’un tapis rouge ou une conférence de presse. Des histoires venues du monde entier, un public à l’écoute Le cinéma présenté à Marrakech ne se limite pas à un seul regard. Les films en compétition et les différentes sections permettent de passer d’un univers à un autre, d’une culture à une autre et parfois d’une réalité sociale à une autre. C’est aussi ce qui fait la particularité du festival : offrir au public la possibilité de sortir de ses habitudes et de découvrir des histoires auxquelles il n’aurait peut-être pas été confronté ailleurs. Cette rencontre entre les œuvres et les spectateurs constitue l’un des fils rouges de la manifestation. Certains films suscitent l’émotion, d’autres interrogent ou divisent, tandis que certains ouvrent simplement une fenêtre sur une autre manière de raconter le monde. Mounir Mehimdate Les stars à Marrakech, mais les spectateurs au premier plan Au fil des jours, Marrakech voit défiler de nombreuses personnalités du cinéma. Acteurs, réalisateurs, producteurs et professionnels viennent présenter leurs films ou échanger avec le public. Mais cette concentration de célébrités ne fait pas disparaître ceux qui donnent son énergie au festival. Dans les salles, les spectateurs restent au centre de l’expérience. Leur présence rappelle que le cinéma, aussi prestigieux soit-il, ne prend véritablement vie qu’au moment où il rencontre un regard. C’est particulièrement visible lors des projections et des rencontres qui permettent aux cinéastes de confronter directement leur travail aux réactions du public. Une relation qui dépasse la simple présentation d’un film pour devenir un véritable échange. Et alors que la 23e édition poursuit son parcours entre projections, rencontres et hommages, Marrakech continue de vivre au rythme des histoires racontées sur grand écran. Dans les salles comme dans les rues, sur les tapis rouges comme parmi les spectateurs, le cinéma s’affiche partout. Et derrière chaque film projeté, il y a un regard pour le recevoir, une émotion pour l’accompagner et un public pour lui donner vie. The post FIFM : À Marrakech, le cinéma se vit aussi dans les regards du public appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: PDP will reclaim Ebonyi in 2027, chairman declares
items.description: …As Odii receives flag, promises economic revival By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki The National Chairman of the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Abdulrahman Mohammed Takushara, has expressed confidence that the party will reclaim Ebonyi State in the 2027 governorship election through its candidate, Chief Ifeanyichukwu Odii. Mohammed stated this in Abakaliki during the campaign flag-off and presentation of flags to Odii and other PDP candidates in the state. He said Ebonyi had remained a PDP stronghold since 1999 until the party lost power, alleging that its mandate was taken away by the ruling party. The national chairman further alleged that the PDP won the last governorship election in the state but was denied victory, insisting that the party would reclaim its mandate in 2027. He urged residents to vote for PDP candidates, saying the party was determined to change the state’s economic fortunes. In his acceptance speech after receiving the party’s flag, Odii criticised Governor Francis Nwifuru’s spending priorities and promised to revive the state’s economy through industrialisation, agriculture and infrastructure development if elected. The PDP candidate accused the Nwifuru administration of failing to translate increased federal allocations into improved living conditions for residents. He said that despite the increase in federal allocations to the state since 2023, poverty, inadequate electricity, poor healthcare, sanitation challenges and limited economic opportunities remained major concerns. Odii cited a national poverty assessment which, he said, indicated that nearly eight out of every 10 Ebonyi residents lived in multidimensional poverty. He also questioned the government’s expenditure priorities, alleging that it spent N19.78 billion on donations, entertainment and refreshments by the third quarter of 2026, while allocating N9 billion to education and healthcare combined. He further alleged that the government spent less than its approved healthcare budget in 2025, while no expenditure was recorded for textbooks and teacher training. He also claimed that agriculture received less than two per cent of the state’s 2025 budget. The businessman said his experience in business and philanthropy had prepared him for the task of governing the state. He said his foundation had built more than 150 homes for less privileged families, awarded scholarships to over 2,500 Nigerians and provided relief materials to more than 40,000 families. According to him, the foundation also supports over 1,000 farmers annually with agricultural inputs and has empowered 3,000 entrepreneurs through grants and seed capital, in addition to executing rural electrification and road projects. Unveiling his development agenda, Odii promised to promote agricultural mechanisation, irrigation, access to finance and agro-processing facilities to improve farmers’ productivity and earnings. He said his administration would pursue an integrated infrastructure programme covering roads, electricity, water, housing and digital connectivity, while encouraging private-sector investment in power generation and renewable energy. The PDP candidate also promised to improve school infrastructure, strengthen teacher development, expand technical and vocational education and promote youth entrepreneurship. On healthcare, he pledged to equip primary healthcare centres, provide essential medicines and recruit qualified medical personnel, particularly in underserved communities. Odii also promised reforms in the civil service, land administration and justice system, as well as improved security coordination and mechanisms for resolving communal disputes. He said his administration would establish delivery units to monitor projects, introduce periodic performance assessments for ministries, departments and agencies, and publish regular reports on government performance. Earlier, Mohammed urged residents to vote for PDP candidates in the National Assembly elections scheduled for January 16, 2027, and support Odii and other party candidates in the governorship and State Assembly elections on February 6. He expressed confidence that the party would reclaim the state, saying, “History will repeat itself in Ebonyi State come February 6.” The PDP chairman urged residents to mobilise support for the party’s candidates in the Senate and House of Representatives elections, describing the PDP as a party that understood the needs and aspirations of the people. Mohammed commended the party’s leadership for providing a platform to strengthen its political activities in the state, particularly acknowledging the role of the Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, Nyesom Wike. He described the reception accorded the party at the campaign flag-off as evidence of its continued strength in Ebonyi. The national chairman expressed optimism that the PDP would win the governorship election, promising that the party’s national leadership would return to the state to celebrate its victory. items.title: One Girl Married Every Three Seconds as World Falls Behind on Promise to End Child Marriage
items.description: Countries: World, Bangladesh, occupied Palestinian territory, Sierra Leone Source: Save the Children LONDON/GENEVA, 27 November 2026 – Nearly one girl every three seconds is married before the age of 18 despite world leaders committing more than 10 years ago to end child marriage by 2030, said Save the Children said on the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage [1] [2] . Save the Children said progress at ending child marriage has slowed to a crawl, leaving millions of girls at risk of being denied their childhoods, education, safety and future opportunities. Global child marriage rates have fallen by just 3.4 percentage points since 2014 , from 21.9% to 18.5%, and have barely shifted in the last two years [3]. At the current pace, the world is dangerously off track to meet its commitment to end child marriage in the next four years with hard-won gains at risk of reversal, said the child rights organisation. The warning comes as conflict, climate shocks, displacement, economic pressures and shrinking international aid budgets push more families towards negative coping mechanisms including marrying off their daughters. According to the Girls Not Brides network, of which Save the Children is a member, 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 each year – around 23 girls married every minute, or 1 girl married every 3 seconds. In Gaza, latest UN data reveals a significant rise in early and forced marriages incidents, with a stark 123% increase between the first two quarters of 2026. While most reported incidents (67%) involved women aged 18- 59, girls aged 12-17 accounted for 16% of cases. Despite the alarming slowdown in progress, Save the Children said countries that have invested consistently in girls’ rights and protection demonstrate that change is possible. In Bangladesh, for example, while nearly half the country’s women aged 20 to 24 were married before age 18, of child marriage rates fell from 62.7% to 47.2% over roughly the same period that global progress stagnated [4]. This was due to no single initiative but sustained political commitment and targeted investments in social protection, girls' education, community-led norm change, prevention and response to gender-based violence, and initiatives that strengthened girls' agency and ability to exercise their rights. Sierra Leone has also demonstrated how sustained advocacy and political commitment can drive progress. Recently, years of advocacy led by girls, communities, civil society organisations and development partners helped secure stronger legal protections for girls, including the adoption of the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2024. Since then, the 2026 “Never Before 18” campaign, supported by Save the Children, has helped maintain public and political attention on ending child marriage by elevating girls' voices, raising awareness of the law, and calling for its effective implementation across the country. Rahinatu Adamu Hussaini, Save the Children’s Global Senior Advisor on gender-based violence prevention and response, said: “Child marriage is not a cultural inevitability or a rite of passage It's a deadline imposed on a girl before she's had the chance to write her own story. It's both a harmful practice, and a form of gender-based violence that violates girls' rights to education, health, bodily autonomy and freedom from violence. “Yet today, nearly one girl every three seconds is married before the age of 18, forced into a harmful practice that cuts short her childhood, limits her choices, and increases her risk of violence, poor health outcomes and lifelong inequality. “That's why this new international day matters. It reminds us that behind every statistic is a girl whose rights, aspirations and future are at stake, at a time when progress is stalling and investment in proven solutions is under threat. " The good news is that we know what works. Child marriage declines when governments invest in girls' education, strengthen social protection systems, prevent and respond to gender-based violence, and create opportunities for girls to participate in decisions that affect their lives. "Countries such as Bangladesh have shown that progress is possible when commitments are matched with sustained investment and accountability. The challenge before us is not a lack of solutions; it is ensuring those solution s reach the girls who need them most." Save the Children is urging governments, donors and international institutions to urgently step up funding for solutions that are proven to reduce child marriage, including education for girls, support for vulnerable families, protection from violence, and opportunities for girls to shape their own futures. Every girl, everywhere, should be able to decide if, when and whom to marry, and to grow up free from violence, coercion and discrimination. NOTES: [1] According to the Girls Not Brides network , of which Save the Children is a member, 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 each year – around 23 girls married every minute, or 1 girl married every 3 seconds. [2] On 4 September 2026, the United Nations General Assembly adopted resolution A/RES/80/309 , proclaiming 27 November as the International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage. The resolution recognizes that these practices violate, abuse or impair human rights and disproportionately affect women and girls, particularly those in vulnerable situations. They can threaten access to education, health, economic opportunities and the full enjoyment of human rights. [3] U NICEF Global Database on Child Marriage / Save the Children Child Atlas data on Child Marriage [4] UNICEF Global Database on Child Marriage / Save the Children Child Atlas (According to UNICEF data, the proportion of women aged 20-24 in Bangladesh who were married before age 18 declined from 62.7% to 47.2%, demonstrating significant progress despite continued challenges. The latest estimate of 47.2% comes from the Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025. ******************************************************************************************************************** For further enquiries please contact: Daphnee Cook Daphnee.cook@savethechildren.org Our media out of hours (BST) contact is media@savethechildren.org.uk / +44(0)7831 650409 Please also check our X account @Save_GlobalNews for news alerts, quotes, statements and location Vlogs.
