items.title: World: From forecasts to action: strengthening Africa's response to El Niño
items.description: Countries: World, Malawi Source: Norwegian Refugee Council As the latest El Niño threatens extreme weather across Africa, NORCAP climate experts are turning weather and climate data into early community defences. By Gifty Baah Published 26. Nov 2026 In Malawi, a farmer listening to a seasonal forecast hears that rainfall is likely to be below normal. But one important question remains unanswered: when should I plant? Plant too early and seeds may fail if the rains stop. Plant too late and crops may not reach maturity. For millions of farmers across Africa, these decisions determine whether families harvest enough food, earn an income, or face hardship. This gap between climate information and decision-making, is where NORCAP's work makes a difference. As Africa faces the impacts of the current El Niño event, NORCAP experts embedded in Regional Climate Centres and National Meteorological and Hydrological Services are contributing to transforming climate data into actionable information. Their support is strengthening forecasting systems, building technical capacity, and improving the early warnings that governments, communities and humanitarian agencies rely on to prepare for climate extremes. What is El Niño? A continent facing growing climate risk El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern characterised by unusually warm surface waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. It weakens trade winds and shifts rainfall patterns, influencing weather conditions across the globe. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) indicates that the current event is almost certain to persist through February 2027 and is forecasted to reach very strong intensity, peaking towards the end of 2026. El Niño typically peaks between November and February, increasing the likelihood of heatwaves, drought, heavy rainfall and other extreme weather in many parts of the world. WMO's October update forecasts record sea-surface temperatures in the Central and Eastern Tropical Pacific. Even during a very strong El Niño, impacts can vary substantially between regions and seasons. Scientists stress that El Niño is natural, but its effects are now unfolding on a planet already made much warmer by human-caused climate change . The contrast from Africa is sharp. ACMAD's September bulletin warns of above normal rainfall and flood risk in the Greater Horn and East Africa, and below normal rainfall in Southern Africa during the main planting season. Floods in West and Central Africa had already affected 1.5 million people in 15 countries by 30th September 2026, displacing 595,000 and killing 533 (OCHA, 2026 as cited by Sandrine). In the Sahel, Climate Impact Lab has projected 66,800 additional heat-related deaths between September 2026 and February 2027 compared with a normal year, with Nigeria (31,400), Sudan (17,500), Niger (10,000) and Chad (8,000) the worst affected. In Madagascar, World Food Programme says 3.7 million people will face crisis-level or worse food insecurity during the October to January lean season (WFP as cited in ACMAD et al., 2026). Building sustainable local expertise Accurate forecasts require more than weather stations and technology. They require skilled people and strong institutions capable of turning data into useful information and ensuring it reaches decision-makers and communities. Across many African countries, national meteorological services continue to face challenges, including limited observation networks, shortages of trained staff, and insufficient resources to maintain and modernise forecasting systems. NORCAP's contribution focuses on addressing these capacity gaps. By embedding experts within climate centres and meteorological services, NORCAP helps partners strengthen forecasting capabilities, improve climate products, and enhance early warning dissemination systems. The approach is long-term and sustainable: building local expertise so institutions can continue improving services independently. The results are already visible. NORCAP's 2025 assessment found that countries using the ClimWeb and CAP Composer platforms issued more than 2,500 per cent more standardised alerts. More than 500 staff from National Meteorological and Hydrological Services received technical training, while the number of African weather stations sharing data internationally increased from 257 to 1,315. The current El Niño event is demonstrating why these investments matter. Malawi: Helping farmers make better decisions In Malawi, NORCAP expert Sinclair Chinyoka has been working with the Department of Climate Change and Meteorological Services (DCCMS) to improve the information available to farmers and decision-makers during the current El Niño event. Recognising that farmers need more than broad seasonal forecasts, Chinyoka helped develop a machine-learning system that predicts the likely onset of rainfall and considers how large-scale climate drivers, including El Niño, affect different parts of the country. He has also strengthened the use of advanced weather-modelling systems to produce localised forecasts and agricultural advisories, while training meteorologists in weather modelling, machine learning and climate forecasting. "Farmers do not simply need to know whether rainfall will be above or below normal. They need information that helps them decide when to plant, what risks to expect, and how to protect their livelihoods. Our goal is to build national capacity so that these services continue to improve long after our support ends," says Chinyoka. The improved forecasts are already helping inform national preparedness efforts. Based on seasonal outlooks produced by department, government agencies have developed contingency plans that include drought-tolerant crops, food reserves, livestock support and flood preparedness measures. While implementation depends on available resources, having advance information allows authorities to act earlier and plan more effectively. ACMAD: Turning climate outlooks into early action At the continental level, NORCAP experts are supporting the African Centre of Meteorological Applications for Development (ACMAD) to translate climate forecasts into practical guidance for governments, humanitarian agencies and development partners. Through the African Continental Climate Outlook Forum (ACCOF), ACMAD works with regional climate centres and national meteorological services to develop seasonal forecasts and risk information for the continent. However, forecasting rainfall is only part of the story. For governments, health agencies and humanitarian organisations, the more important question is what those forecasts mean for communities and livelihoods. NORCAP expert Wendalasida Sandrine works with ACMAD and has contributed to strengthening efforts to produce impact-based climate information and guidance that enables action before disasters strike. "The real value of a forecast is not in predicting the weather. It is in understanding what that weather could mean for crops, water supplies, health systems and vulnerable populations. Our focus is helping decision-makers move from awareness to action," says Sandrine . NORCAP experts have also supported the development of health-focused seasonal outlooks, strengthened drought-monitoring systems, and helped improve forecasting approaches to make them more objective, robust and reliable. These products are informing preparedness discussions not only among technical agencies, but also at ministerial and policy levels across the continent. ICPAC: Understanding why risks are emerging In Eastern Africa, NORCAP supports the IGAD Climate Prediction and Applications Centre (ICPAC) in enhancing its ability to understand and communicate climate risks. Working through the CRAF'D project, NORCAP-experts developed an innovative forecasting approach that goes beyond showing what might happen, to explain why risks are emerging. The system combines multiple sources of scientific evidence to assess rainfall hazards, identify key drivers and communicate uncertainty more clearly. For forecasters and disaster managers, this provides deeper insight into evolving risks and supports more informed decision-making. Importantly, recent analyses highlighted that although El Niño increased the likelihood of wetter conditions, rainfall patterns remained uneven in some areas. The findings reinforced the importance of continuous monitoring and real-time analysis, helping forecasters and disaster management agencies refine their assessments and preparedness measures as conditions evolve. "Decision-makers need to understand not only what the forecast says, but also how confident we are and what factors are driving the risk," explains Nishadh Kalladath , Data Science and Machine Learning Expert at ICPAC. "That additional context supports better planning and more informed early action." From forecast to action Despite significant progress, experts agree that forecasting is only one part of the solution. The greatest challenge is ensuring that warnings reach communities in time and in forms people can understand and use. "Producing forecasts is no longer the hardest part. Making sure they lead to action is," says Sandrine . For farmers, information on the timing of rainfall, dry spells and the end of the season is often more useful than seasonal rainfall totals. Communities also need access to trusted communication channels, local-language advisories, extension services and resources that allow them to act on warnings. NORCAP Regional Adviser, Owiti Zablone, emphasises that climate forecasts should support practical preparedness measures rather than create alarm. "A forecast is not a prediction of destiny. It is a tool for informed decision-making. When people receive timely, reliable climate information, they can take low-regret actions that strengthen resilience regardless of how the season unfolds," says Owiti . These actions may include protecting water sources, preparing drainage systems, conserving soil moisture, or adopting drought-tolerant crops. But climate information alone is not enough. Farmers also need access to seeds, irrigation, finance and extension support. Communities need warnings delivered through trusted channels and local languages. Governments need systems that connect forecasts to preparedness and response mechanisms. This is why NORCAP's support focuses not only on improving forecasts, but also on strengthening the institutions and partnerships required to turn information into action. Investing in resilience before disaster strikes The current El Niño event is providing a real-world test of Africa's climate services and early warning systems. Across Malawi, ACMAD, ICPAC and many other partner institutions, stronger forecasting capabilities are helping governments and communities better understand risks, prepare earlier and make more informed decisions. The benefits extend beyond this year's El Niño. Stronger climate services improve food security, support disaster risk reduction, protect livelihoods and contribute to social stability. They also help countries adapt to a future in which climate extremes are becoming more frequent and more intense. As Sandrine reflects: "Preparing for El Niño is really about preparing for a more extreme future. Every investment in climate services and early warning systems today is an investment in protecting lives, livelihoods and resilience tomorrow."

items.title: Over 380,000 Displaced from Sudan’s Kordofan as Violence Forces Thousands More to Flee
items.description: Country: Sudan Source: International Organization for Migration Khartoum, 26 November 2026 – More than 383,000 people were displaced from Sudan’s Kordofan region between October 2025 and October 2026, with renewed insecurity forcing a further 15,000 people to flee in November alone. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) warns that successive waves of displacement are deepening an already severe humanitarian crisis, leaving thousands of families without safe shelter, access to basic services or the means to support themselves. “Families across Kordofan are being forced to flee time and again, while the communities taking them in are already struggling to meet their own basic needs,” said Mohamed Refaat, IOM Chief of Mission in Sudan. “Civilians must be protected. As more people are forced from their homes, we urgently need the resources and safe access to reach them before their situation deteriorates even further.” West Kordofan has been particularly hard hit by the latest wave of displacement. In November alone, IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) recorded 21 displacement incidents across the region, forcing an estimated 15,310 people from their homes. Nearly 90 per cent of these displacements originated in West Kordofan, with some 12,720 people forced to flee Abu Zabad locality alone. Many families have been forced to move repeatedly, exhausting their already limited resources and disrupting access to healthcare, education and other essential services. The growing number of people seeking refuge in North Kordofan, White Nile and Khartoum is placing additional pressure on host communities and overstretched services. Humanitarian conditions are particularly concerning in West Kordofan, where 70 per cent of households surveyed as part of IOM’s 2026 Multi-Sector Needs Assessment reported protection needs, while access to healthcare and education remained severely constrained. Across Sudan, 38 per cent of surveyed households reported unmet shelter needs. In Kordofan, repeated displacement, damage to homes and the loss of essential belongings have left many families without adequate or safe shelter. IOM continues to track displacement across Kordofan and other affected areas of Sudan to identify emerging needs and guide humanitarian response efforts. Working with partners, IOM is supporting efforts to deliver emergency assistance, including shelter, essential household items and other critical services. As insecurity continues to drive displacement across Kordofan, IOM calls for the protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, safe and unhindered humanitarian access, and urgent additional funding to meet growing needs. Without immediate support, thousands more families risk being left without the assistance they need to survive. Notes to Editors During November 2026, IOM recorded 21 displacement incidents across the Kordofan region, displacing an estimated 15,310 people. Sixteen of these incidents were recorded in West Kordofan, where an estimated 13,515 people were displaced. The figures are based on IOM’s Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM) field reports. The humanitarian needs cited in this release are drawn from IOM’s 2026 Sudan Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA) . The assessment provides a broader picture of humanitarian needs in West Kordofan and should not be interpreted as an assessment of the 12,720 people recently displaced in Abu Zabad locality. Further information on recent displacement in Abu Zabad locality is available through IOM DTM Sudan Flash Alerts: Abu Zabad town , Abu Galib village , and multiple villages in Abu Zabad locality . Editors are encouraged to use recent IOM footage from Sudan to complement their coverage of the crisis, available to view and download on UNifeed . For more information, please visit IOM’s Media Centre .

items.title: Mozambique Conflict Monitor: Almost 10 years into the insurgency, ISM threatens to expand
items.description: Country: Mozambique Source: Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Please refer to the attached file. ISM’s sustained and increasing presence in Mozambique will significantly impact security sector reform, strategic investments, and the movement of people and goods. Author Peter Bofin Regional Expert, Southeast Africa Executive summary As the insurgency in Mozambique enters its 10th year and the end of two years of President Daniel Chapo’s administration draws near, Islamic State Mozambique’s (ISM) actions continue to shape people’s lives across Cabo Delgado province. Despite the continuing presence of the Rwanda Defence Force (RDF) and the support it provides to the Defense Armed Forces of Mozambique (FADM), in the past two years, ISM has broadened its footprint into Niassa and Nampula provinces, while remaining entrenched in Cabo Delgado’s northeast. ISM’s increasing activity in the north, south, and west of Cabo Delgado, as well as in Niassa and Nampula provinces, has been driven by three factors: its need to diversify funding, stretch security forces’ limited capacity, and secure supply lines for recruits and other supplies. As ISM has become more dependent on generating its own finances, the most likely outcome is that these trends continue into the insurgency’s 10th year. This will mean continued hindrance to humanitarian work in the province and further postponements in the reconstruction of public administration and economic revival. Current conflict context ISM has expanded its operations to become self-reliant Throughout 2025 and 2026, ISM has become more reliant on financing from artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM), kidnapping for ransom, and extortion on roads. These sources of income have become a financial imperative for the group as external financing has declined due to recent United States and United Arab Emirates airstrikes against the Islamic State (IS) Somalia province, which finances IS internationally. Recent evidence underscores that the push for self-reliance has been driving ISM’s behavior over the past six months, leading to more frequent activity outside its heartland of Macomia, Mocímboa da Praia, and Muidumbe districts ( see map below ). To the west, the group was present in the Montepuez and Balama districts in each of the six months from May to October, where it carried out a single operation from July to October. It has also maintained a presence to the south, where it exerted control over gold- and gemstone-producing areas in Meluco and Ancuabe districts, and maintained links to Nampula province through Chiúre district. To the north, it has become increasingly active in Nangade district, along the border with Tanzania, likely to maintain links with support networks north of the border. ISM is sustaining its presence in the west In the west, ISM has been active in Montepuez district and has threatened both Niassa province to the west and Balama and Namuno districts to the south. From July through October, it conducted significant operations in Montepuez’s Nairoto area, where it exerted control over ASM gold mining sites, undertook one sortie into Niassa province, and restricted traffic on the R698 road from Montepuez to Mueda by setting up roadblocks ( see map below ). This was not ISM’s first sortie to Nairoto. However, its ability to sustain a presence there from July to October suggests it has knowledge and support networks in the area that could support a more permanent presence. The group was based at the Shamba Kubwa gold mining area in the north of Nairoto for most of September and could move freely in Montepuez district and south to Balama district. ISM’s operations in the west of Cabo Delgado have been its most lucrative thus far. In October, it received over $50,000 in ransom for a South African man the group kidnapped in a raid on a hunting camp in Niassa province the previous month and held in Shamba Kubwa for most of September. According to local sources, much of the ransom was paid in cryptocurrency because the sum was too large for mobile money platforms. Extortion at roadblocks and ransoms paid for Mozambicans captured in village raids are paid through mobile money accounts on Mozambican telecom platforms. ISM’s now-confirmed use of cryptocurrency significantly complicates efforts to control ISM’s access to finance. The insurgency has maintained its links to Tanzania To the north, renewed activity in Nangade district in September and October has been modest: ISM has been involved in just seven violent incidents. According to local sources, ISM’s presence is thought to reflect ongoing connections to support networks in Tanzania; the group has been present in the district up to five times each year since 2024. The insurgency has had links to Tanzania since its beginning in 2017, and ISM’s current leader, Sheikh Hassan Ulanga, is originally from Tanzania. Attacks on villages, particularly to the south of the district, regularly displace civilians and place pressure on civic and military authorities, which can create openings for movement of people across the border. Such movements — which occur along the border in Nangade district and in western Mueda district — likely include active fighters temporarily moving to Tanzania, new recruits coming to Mozambique, and possible cash movements into or out of Mozambique. This continues despite the presence of Tanzanian forces on both sides of the border. Typically, recruits entering Mozambique are met at the border by ISM fighters, before being moved to bases further south. ISM insurgents target southern Cabo Delgado for gold and recruits ISM’s behavior in southern Cabo Delgado has been similarly episodic. While not established there, the group undertakes regular violent sorties into the Meluco, Ancuabe, Chiúre, and Namuno districts, as well as into Nampula province ( see map below ). As in Montepuez, the group has spent significant time south in recent months. Its most significant recent operation lasted two months , and is its longest-lasting operation in the province’s southern districts so far. As in the west, ISM has multiple objectives in carrying out its operations in the south. First, they allow the group to extort miners and buyers at ASM gold and gemstone mining sites in Ancuabe, Meluco, and Namuno districts. Second, they can help new recruits move north out of Nampula and may serve as a channel for moving gold to markets in Nampula, according to sources in the province. Movements south are also notable for the sites that ISM does not target. The group does not mount roadblocks on the east-west N1 and N14 roads, nor does it target vulnerable military positions in the south, such as the FADM camp at Macarara close to the N14, or the nearby RDF position at Nacololo. This suggests that ISM has no intention of exerting control over territory between those roads and Nampula, and that its focus is on maintaining links with supporters in Nampula. State response State forces, including FADM, the RDF, and the Tanzania People’s Defence Force (TPDF), have not matched ISM’s sustained and distributed activity or its mobility over the past six months. FADM operates under capacity constraints, despite international support. The RDF has had some success with its narrower mandate of ensuring security conditions allow the liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects in the country to proceed. Tanzania’s principal concern of ensuring that the conflict does not spill over its border is an objective it is successfully fulfilling. FADM carries out limited operations against ISM FADM’s engagements with ISM have been mostly concentrated in the east, both on land and in nearshore waters, with limited activity to the west, despite ISM’s push into Montepuez and Balama districts from July to October ( see map below ). In July, FADM moved the operational command of the Northern Operational Theater of the Defense and Security Forces from Pemba to Mocímboa da Praia. The following month, Mocímboa da Praia’s airport was closed to civilian traffic , though it is still active militarily and provides air support to RDF operations in northern Macomia district. The closure of the airport has significantly restricted humanitarian operations in the town. Despite FADM’s heightened presence, ISM remains active in villages around the town. Both FADM and the RDF are reluctant to respond to the movements of small groups of ISM insurgents in villages around the town and instead focus on breaking up ISM support networks in the town, on which the group depends for food and other supplies. Most notable is FADM’s lack of engagement with ISM west of the N380 across Macomia and Meluco districts. For ISM, this is strategically important territory. The group targets communities in western Macomia by looting them to support fighters across that district. Meluco is important for two reasons. Firstly, the Messalo River corridor provides access to Montepuez and Balama districts. Secondly, over the past two years, ISM has successfully sought to control artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) in Meluco as a source of income. International partners: The RDF and TPDF have adopted a less aggressive posture In the past six months, both the RDF and the TPDF have restricted their activity to areas of greatest strategic interest. The RDF has focused on degrading ISM positions south of Mocímboa da Praia, particularly in the Quiterajo and Mbau area, where ISM maintains a stronghold. Given the RDF’s mission to protect the LNG project further north, its priority is to minimize ISM’s impact on the project’s operations ( see map below ). Elsewhere in the province, the RDF has continued to take a less aggressive posture, despite having at least one base on the N380 road in Macomia district and another in Ancuabe district near the N14 road. There, the RDF’s long-standing reluctance to respond to ISM operations continues. The TPDF is based in Nangade town and Mandimba village, east of Nangade district, and it has at least three positions on the other side of the Mozambique-Tanzania border facing Cabo Delgado. Despite ISM’s increased activity in the Nangade district in recent months, ACLED records just one clash in the past six months between the TPDF and ISM, thought locally to be related to supporting cross-border movements of people and possibly supplies. The TPDF’s quieter posture is consistent with Tanzania’s now-established preference for a less interventionist approach in the region and prioritizing its own domestic security. A consequence of this less interventionist approach is that it doesn’t undermine the status quo. Outlook ISM has continued to be adaptive in the past six months, as evidenced in its increasing presence and influence in the west, its more sustained presence in the province’s southern districts, and its continued ability to operate along the Tanzanian border when it chooses to do so. State forces’ response has been less adaptive; FADM, in particular, has been at best reactive in the west, while ignoring the Messalo River corridor. The RDF is restricted in its mandate to remain focused on the east to protect the LNG project in Palma over the long term. This configuration is likely to continue into 2027, with significant consequences for the movement of people and goods, security sector reform, and strategic investments. ISM poses a threat to the flow of people and goods The N380 highway, which runs through the heart of the near 10-year-long conflict, will remain open to commercial traffic, though with a high risk that ISM will effectively impose tolls through roadblocks. Driven by commercial interests, businesses will continue to limit exposure to violence on this road through paying off ISM, either at ad hoc roadblocks, which put people and goods at risk, or through anticipatory payments. ISM’s westward move will also make such practices a cost of doing business on the R698, the Montepuez-Mueda route in the west. The greater impact will be on humanitarian organizations, which have not been in a position to make such arrangements on the N380 and will similarly not be able to do so on the R698. This will restrict support to internally displaced people and returnees in Mocímboa da Praia, Mueda, and Nangade, as well as the revival of public services and the economy in the north. Security sector reform is necessary to address the ISM threat Rwanda remains a stable partner and is likely to maintain a presence in Mozambique until at least 2029, the projected year of first production from the TotalEnergies LNG project. FADM and the Ministry of Defense are well-established as the primary points of contact for support, having taken the lead role in the security response from the police in 2021. Nevertheless, security sector reform partners face three key issues that will impact the security response in the coming year as ISM develops a new center of gravity to the west and presents a sustained threat to the north and south. First, a centralized command structure has slowed troops’ response times in the field. The issue is particularly acute given that ISM prefers to operate in small, mobile groups. Second, there is a need for better intelligence. Finally, logistical and financial obstacles to supporting effective military operations also contribute to slow response times. These issues will be a priority for international partners such as the European Union and the US government in the coming months. Supporting intelligence-led, decentralized command and control within FADM is a priority for the EU Military Assistance Mission in Mozambique (EUMAMM). If successful, this will likely be reflected in more dynamic FADM action in areas in Montepuez and, if necessary, Niassa, as well as in Cabo Delgado’s southern districts. US support is focused on the police, particularly on improving security on the N380 and the N1 roads. A key indicator of success on these routes will be increased humanitarian traffic, particularly on the N380. Strategic investments will drive interest in Mozambique Security sector reform is bound tightly to national and international strategic interests. Northern Mozambique’s natural resources make it of considerable interest to Mozambique itself, its neighbors, and international powers. In 2027, some change can be expected in how these interests are addressed. The critical projects relate to the Eni, TotalEnergies, and ExxonMobil LNG projects. The latter two, being onshore, drive the RDF deployment, while the TotalEnergies-led project is instrumental in European security sector support. As ExxonMobil approaches its final investment decision on its own onshore LNG project, the US is seeking to expand security sector cooperation through agreed support for the police and proposed support to FADM. If the US gets the green light to undertake Joint Combined Exchange Training in Mozambique in 2027, it will signal heightened US influence with the current administration. Mining investments will continue to remain at risk. Existing graphite projects in Balama district in Cabo Delgado and Niassa’s Nipepe district will continue. However, as ISM becomes more active in Montepuez, this will pose potential security risks to facilities and main transport routes. As-yet-undeveloped concessions in Balama and Montepuez will likely face considerable delays in attracting financing for development. If Niassa Reserve boundaries are redrawn to accommodate mining interests, ISM’s continued presence in Montepuez presents a greater threat to Niassa province, threatening existing tourism and conservation interests and potential future mining projects. Finally, more sustained ISM activity in western Cabo Delgado will be most acutely felt by civilian communities, which will become increasingly hard to reach with humanitarian assistance. It is highly likely that ISM will increasingly gain control of gold resources unless the state can take credible steps to reduce ISM’s influence on the sector through a coordinated approach involving security and other actions such as tackling financing mechanisms and logistics networks. In the next year, FADM operations in the Messalo River corridor will be both necessary and essential to addressing this issue and controlling ISM’s growing influence. This report was produced as part of the Mozambique Conflict Monitor in collaboration with Zitamar News .

items.title: Crew member dies after diesel tanker capsizes off Ibiza, no pollution so far
items.description: MADRID, Nov 26 (Reuters) - At least one crew member aboard a ship carrying diesel has died after the vessel capsized and partially sank off the Spanish island of Ibiza on Thursday, regional authorities said, adding there were no signs of pollution so far. The Malta-flagged chemical tanker Med Emre was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona and may have been carrying up to 7,000 metric tons of diesel when it keeled over about 30 nautical miles (56 km) off Ibiza's northwestern coast, the Balearic Islands' interior department said.

items.title: Ireland men set for maiden tour of Pakistan in January, to play three ODIs
items.description: The Ireland men’s team will tour Pakistan in January for the first time to play three One-day Internationals against the hosts, the cricket boards of both countries announced on Thursday. The visitors, according to the Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB), are scheduled to arrive in the country on Jan 9, and will take on national developmental side Pakistan Shaheens for three warm-up one-day matches between Jan 13 and 17. The ODIs are set for Jan 20, 22 and 24. All six matches, the PCB said, will be played at Lahore’s Gaddafi Stadium. The series was originally planned to be a multi-format one before plans were changed with the proximity of the 2027 World Cup in mind. “While we originally planned a multi-format series, both Boards have agreed that their respective squads would benefit most from playing 50-over cricket given our upcoming participation in the World Cup Qualifier and Pakistan preparing for the World Cup itself later in 2027,” Graeme West, Director of High Performance at Cricket Ireland, said in a statement. This tour, therefore, is an important milestone for Ireland, who are also all set to feature in the upcoming World Cup Qualifier, through which they’ll try to secure their spot for next year’s showpiece. “Over the years we have enjoyed a close relationship with the Pakistan Cricket Board and their players, and we look forward to this historic first tour – the first of many in the coming years, we hope,” West added. For the hosts, meanwhile, the tour would be an opportunity to test their depth – especially through the Shaheens matches – and continue the fine-tuning process of their combinations ahead of the World Cup. Pakistan made a statement of sorts about their ODI form, convincingly winning a tri-series, which featured England and Sri Lanka along with Shaheen Shah Afridi’s side. Correction: An earlier version of this story stated that the Ireland team would be arriving next month. The error is regretted.

items.title: Fonds souverain de Guinée : « épargner pour les générations futures, nos enfants, nos petits-enfants. Car la richesse des mines est épuisable », dit Mariama Ciré Sylla
items.description: Après l’adoption par les députés du projet de loi portant création, organisation et fonctionnement du Fonds souverain de la République de Guinée, le 25 novembre 2026, la ministre de l’Économie, des Finances et du Budget, Mariama Ciré Sylla, a précisé les ambitions de cet instrument financier. Selon elle, le dispositif permettra notamment d’épargner une partie des revenus miniers, de protéger l’économie nationale contre les crises économiques, de financer des secteurs stratégiques et de constituer un patrimoine au profit des générations futures. Au sortir de la plénière de l’Assemblée nationale, tenue mercredi 25 novembre à l’hémicycle, la ministre a qualifié l’adoption de ce texte de moment historique pour la Guinée. Elle y voit l’aboutissement d’un processus de réformes engagé depuis plusieurs années et une étape importante dans la volonté des autorités de faire bénéficier les générations présentes et futures des richesses du sous-sol guinéen. Prenant la parole devant les médias, Mariama Ciré Sylla a d’abord rendu hommage au président de la République, le général Mamadi Doumbouya, pour sa vision et son ambition en faveur de la valorisation des ressources nationales. « C’est un grand jour encore une fois pour notre nation, pour nos populations et surtout pour nos enfants. Je voudrais commencer par rendre un hommage appuyé à Son Excellence, Monsieur le Président de la République, pour sa vision, pour son leadership et son ambition de faire que chaque richesse du sous-sol guinéen puisse bénéficier à nos citoyens », a-t-elle déclaré. Elle a également remercié le Premier ministre, chef du gouvernement, le Comité stratégique Simandou, les différents départements ministériels ayant contribué à l’élaboration du texte, ainsi que la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée. Selon la ministre, la création du Fonds souverain s’inscrit dans une dynamique plus large de transformation économique et institutionnelle engagée par les autorités guinéennes. « Ce projet de loi est l’aboutissement d’une vision qui n’a pas commencé hier. Ces dernières années, comme vous avez remarqué, beaucoup de réformes ont été faites avec la création du Delivery Unit, la création de la Guinea Development Board pour attirer le secteur privé, avec la loi Plan et Programme Simandou 2040 pour mettre en place un programme qui va nous permettre, pour les 15 prochaines années, de développer notre pays, mais aussi avec d’autres réformes comme la digitalisation des impôts qui nous ont permis de multiplier nos revenus », a-t-elle expliqué. La ministre a également évoqué l’adoption récente du programme économique et financier de la Guinée par le Fonds monétaire international (FMI), estimant que l’ensemble de ces réformes vise à mieux valoriser les ressources naturelles du pays. Abordant le fonctionnement du Fonds souverain, Mariama Ciré Sylla a expliqué que celui-ci sera alimenté notamment par une partie des revenus issus du projet Simandou et des futurs projets miniers. « Le Fonds souverain, c’est cet outil qui va nous permettre de mettre de côté une partie des revenus du Simandou, 30 %, mais aussi une partie, 5 %, des revenus des futurs projets miniers, afin qu’on puisse épargner et investir pour l’État », a-t-elle précisé. Au-delà de sa vocation d’investissement, la ministre a insisté sur la dimension intergénérationnelle de ce mécanisme. Elle estime que la Guinée fait ainsi le choix de ne pas consacrer l’ensemble de ses ressources aux dépenses immédiates, mais également de constituer une épargne pour l’avenir. « C’est la première fois que la République de Guinée a dit : non, nous, on veut non seulement investir, mais aussi épargner pour les générations futures. Donc, ce Fonds-là, c’est un outil financier qui va nous permettre de mettre de côté de l’argent, premièrement, pour protéger notre économie contre les chocs ou les situations de crise économique qui peuvent arriver », a-t-elle souligné. Le dispositif devra également contribuer au financement de secteurs jugés stratégiques, notamment l’agriculture et l’énergie, avec pour objectif de stimuler la création d’emplois et de richesses. « Deuxièmement, permettre à notre pays d’investir dans des secteurs stratégiques, l’agriculture, l’énergie, afin de créer de l’emploi et de la richesse pour les Guinéens. Et troisièmement, épargner pour les générations futures, nos enfants, nos petits-enfants. Car la richesse des mines est épuisable, mais si on investit dans l’éducation, dans le capital, même si on construit des infrastructures, si on arrive à développer notre pays, à le rendre prospère, c’est ça qui reste », a-t-elle développé. Satisfaite de l’adoption du texte, Mariama Ciré Sylla a annoncé que la prochaine étape sera consacrée à la mise en œuvre et à l’opérationnalisation effective du Fonds. Elle a, à cet égard, assuré que des mécanismes de gouvernance et de contrôle ont été prévus pour garantir une gestion transparente et rigoureuse. La ministre a également salué les contributions et observations formulées par les députés lors de l’examen du projet de loi, estimant qu’elles ont permis d’enrichir le texte. Pour illustrer le potentiel de cet instrument, elle a cité les expériences de la Norvège et du Botswana, deux pays disposant de mécanismes souverains d’épargne et d’investissement. « À titre d’exemple, le Fonds norvégien a aujourd’hui 2 300 milliards en termes de ressources. Et croyez-moi, plus de deux tiers de ces ressources-là ne viennent pas des revenus du pétrole, qui originellement étaient les revenus qui ont permis de l’abonder, mais plutôt des investissements qu’il a faits. Au Botswana, on a un Fonds similaire. C’est notre ambition que la Guinée puisse fructifier les ressources des mines, en faire un patrimoine, un capital pour non seulement la génération présente, mais celle à venir. C’est toute la vision de Son Excellence Monsieur le Président de la République », a-t-elle conclu. Mamadou Yaya Barry L’article Fonds souverain de Guinée : « épargner pour les générations futures, nos enfants, nos petits-enfants. Car la richesse des mines est épuisable », dit Mariama Ciré Sylla est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Souveraineté sanitaire dans l’espace AES : La deuxième édition du SIPSIS s’ouvre à Ouagadougou
items.description: La deuxième édition du Salon international des professionnels de santé et d’intégration des soins (SIPSIS) s’est ouverte le 25 novembre 2026, à Ouagadougou. Placée sous le thème des défis sanitaires de la décennie 2027-2036, cette rencontre réunit le Burkina Faso, le Mali et le Niger autour d’un objectif commun : renforcer la souveraineté sanitaire de l’espace AES. Après une première édition organisée en 2024, le SIPSIS revient avec l’ambition de créer un cadre d’échanges entre les acteurs du secteur de la santé. Jusqu’au 27 novembre, des panels et des rencontres permettront aux professionnels de réfléchir aux solutions pour mieux répondre aux besoins sanitaires des populations au cours des dix prochaines années. Dans son discours prononcé au nom du chef de l’État, Émile Zerbo, ministre d’État, ministre de l’Administration territoriale et de la Mobilité, a rappelé que la souveraineté sanitaire passe par la capacité des États à définir leurs priorités, à mobiliser des financements et à garantir l’accès aux soins, même dans les zones les plus éloignées. Il a également insisté sur l’importance de la production locale des produits de santé. « Produire localement les produits de santé dont notre peuple a besoin relève d’un choix de souveraineté. Cet effort rappelle la mutualisation de nos compétences, la mobilisation de nos financements et la pleine participation de notre jeunesse » , a-t-il déclaré. Pour Ésaïe Kindo, secrétaire général du SIPSIS, cette deuxième édition vise à mobiliser l’ensemble des acteurs du secteur de la santé autour de la souveraineté sanitaire. L’objectif est également d’anticiper les défis sanitaires de la prochaine décennie et de proposer des réponses adaptées aux réalités des pays participants. À travers cette rencontre, le SIPSIS entend ainsi encourager la coopération entre les pays de l’AES et favoriser des actions communes pour construire des systèmes de santé plus solides et accessibles aux populations. L’article Souveraineté sanitaire dans l’espace AES : La deuxième édition du SIPSIS s’ouvre à Ouagadougou est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Attaque contre deux navires russes en Libye : l’Algérie réagit
items.description: L’Algérie a réagi ce jeudi aux attaques perpétrées par l’Ukraine contre deux navires russes dont un militaire à Benghazi, en Libye , dimanche 22 novembre. Pour la Libye, les « récents développements, et notamment les attaques ayant visé le port de Benghazi, ne peuvent susciter de notre part que condamnation et réprobation », a déclaré ce jeudi en conférence de presse le ministre des Affaires étrangères Ahmed Attaf. Ces attaques revendiquées par l’Ukraine constituent une « violation de la souveraineté » de la Libye et une « atteinte inacceptable à l'inviolabilité de son territoire », a dénoncé le chef de la diplomatie algérienne. L’Algérie appelle les Libyens à « s'engager dans un processus politique inclusif » Pour M. Attaf, les attaques ukrainiennes contre des navires russes en Libye illustrent de « manière flagrante le besoin pressant, non seulement sur le plan politique, mais aussi affectif et humain, de parvenir à une solution qui mette fin à la crise et aux souffrances du peuple libyen ». Dans ce contexte, l'Algérie appelle à faire « prévaloir l'intérêt national supérieur », à mettre de côté les « différends entre frères » et à « s'engager dans un processus politique inclusif, qui débouche sur des institutions unifiées et légitimes et permette au peuple libyen de décider de son avenir, loin des diktats, des ingérences étrangères et de la logique des règlements provisoires, qui ne mettent pas durablement la Libye sœur à l'abri des risques d'aggravation des divisions et d'intensification de l'escalade », a ajouté M. Attaf. L’article Attaque contre deux navires russes en Libye : l’Algérie réagit est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Yemen: Calling for Collective Action and Resource Mobilization to Scale Up the Urgent Humanitarian Response
items.description: Country: Yemen Source: Life for Relief and Development 369,000 internally displaced people need essential humanitarian assistance to survive. Taiz and Lahj are among the leading governorates of origin for displaced families, requiring intensified relief efforts. Women and children are among the groups most severely affected by the conflict. Internal displacement continues across Yemen amid the escalating consequences of the conflict and mounting humanitarian pressures on affected families. According to the International Organization for Migration (IOM) Yemen report released this month, 369,012 people, representing 61,502 households, have been displaced this year. The report indicates that Taiz was the leading governorate of origin for displaced people during the monitoring period, accounting for 48% of the total, followed by Lahj at 45% and Al Hudaydah at 3%. The remaining 4% came from several other governorates, including Marib, Al Dhale'e, Ibb, Aden, Abyan, Sana'a, Hajjah, Shabwah, Al Bayda, Al Jawf, Al Mahwit, Dhamar, and Hadramout. Women and Children Among the Most Severely Affected In response to this escalating humanitarian crisis, numerous relief organizations have launched initiatives to support those in need. To gain a closer understanding of conditions on the ground, we spoke with Eng. Mabrouk Shubail, Director of LIFE for Relief and Development's office in Yemen, about the humanitarian situation, the challenges facing displaced families, and the difficulties confronting humanitarian workers. The following is our interview: To begin, could you explain the reality of the humanitarian situation in Yemen following the escalation of political tensions in the region? Certainly. According to the United Nations' 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan and UNICEF, approximately 22.3 million people in Yemen require humanitarian assistance, including 10.95 million women and girls in need of assistance and protection. Approximately 2.2 million children under the age of five are suffering from acute malnutrition, while 1.3 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are at risk of malnutrition. More than 7 million children also face increased protection risks, while approximately 4.5 million children have been deprived of education. These figures reflect the extensive humanitarian consequences of the conflict, particularly for women and children. Protection assessments reveal specific risks facing women and children. Why are these groups particularly vulnerable? In general, women and children living in conflict and displacement settings face overlapping humanitarian, health, psychological, and social risks. Their suffering extends far beyond losing their homes or fleeing areas of active fighting. It also includes threats to their physical safety, restricted access to essential services, and exposure to various forms of violence, exploitation, and harassment in unsafe shelter environments. As conditions in Yemen continue to deteriorate, an increasing number of households are being headed by women. Repeated displacement further intensifies their suffering, particularly due to the lack of adequate shelter, overcrowding in available accommodation, and limited living space. Additional health risks arise from chronic illnesses affecting some family members, the spread of communicable diseases, and gaps in vaccination coverage. There is also a critical shortage of psychological first aid and crisis counseling services, which are essential early interventions for protecting vulnerable populations. How do you assess the relief needs of displaced families? As the humanitarian situation in Yemen deteriorates following the renewed conflict, many families have lost their homes and possessions. This has increased the urgent need for humanitarian interventions that provide shelter to displaced and affected households, improve their living conditions, ease their suffering, and strengthen their ability to cope with the consequences of displacement. The Executive Unit for the Management of Displacement Camps, operating under the Yemeni Prime Minister's Office, has identified several essential humanitarian needs facing displaced families that require urgent intervention. These include: Food Assistance: Providing food and essential supplies to affected households. Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH): Ensuring access to safe water, hygiene supplies, and adequate sanitation facilities. Healthcare: Providing displaced people with essential medical services and healthcare. Shelter and Accommodation: Supplying suitable housing and shelter materials to protect families from harsh living conditions. Protection: Strengthening protection measures for displaced populations, particularly the most vulnerable groups. Livelihoods and Cash Assistance: Supporting families in restoring their ability to meet their basic living needs. In light of these indicators, the report issued an urgent appeal to mobilize funding and resources and strengthen operational capacities, with the aim of expanding the coordinated humanitarian response and providing the necessary assistance to displaced households. How can humanitarian workers determine priorities when dealing with such a massive number of people in need? The fundamental responsibility of humanitarian workers is to provide people with the basic necessities required for survival. The expanding scale of displacement, with affected families spread across ten governorates and 59 districts, makes stronger coordination among relief organizations and intensified joint efforts essential to meeting growing needs and ensuring that assistance reaches the most vulnerable households. We have made considerable efforts to identify areas that have not yet received humanitarian assistance, assess the most vulnerable cases, and determine their specific needs. Our planned assistance in Taiz and Lahj includes support for displacement camps and the provision of essential household items. These supplies include mattresses and foam pillows, large sleeping mattresses, floor mats, two-burner gas stoves and cooking utensils, dining plates, two-gallon water containers, 20-liter water buckets, and 25-liter gas cylinders. As an initial step, we have worked to support approximately 600 families and are currently identifying additional highly vulnerable households to expand the scope of our assistance. As Director of LIFE for Relief and Development's office in Yemen, what challenges are you facing? Some of the challenges exceed what a single relief organization can address independently and require collective action and cooperation among all stakeholders. The scale of need is enormous due to the growing number of people affected by the widening conflict. Reaching the poorest and most vulnerable households requires coordinated efforts, as does reviewing and verifying beneficiary lists to exclude individuals who have not been directly affected and ensuring that assistance is delivered directly to beneficiaries in the field. Nevertheless, we believe these challenges can be addressed. LIFE has been operating in Yemen for 34 years. This longstanding presence has enabled us to develop an in-depth understanding of the country's conditions, the nature of humanitarian needs, and the challenges facing affected communities. We therefore work simultaneously across different areas through our teams deployed in several governorates. These teams coordinate closely to accelerate needs assessments and ensure the timely implementation of relief activities. For more information: https://lifeusa.org/#social-media

items.title: Labé : un court-circuit provoque un incendie qui ravage plusieurs chambres à Daka 1
items.description: Un incendie s’est déclaré dans l’après-midi du mercredi 25 novembre 2026 dans une concession située au quartier Daka 1, dans la commune urbaine de Labé. Le sinistre, qui serait d’origine électrique, a entièrement consumé plusieurs chambres, occasionnant d’importants dégâts matériels. Aucune perte en vie humaine ni blessé n’a été enregistré. Selon les informations recueillies sur place, les flammes ont ravagé plusieurs pièces de la concession, causant d’importantes pertes matérielles à la famille sinistrée. Interrogé par notre correspondant régional, Mamadou Dian Diallo, membre de la famille victime, est revenu sur les circonstances de l’alerte et les premières tentatives d’intervention. « C’est aux environs de 16 heures. Moi, j’étais dans l’autre bâtiment, en face, avec mon père. Un court-circuit s’est produit dans le bâtiment voisin. Quelqu’un qui s’en est rendu compte est venu frapper à notre porte pour nous alerter. Je suis alors sorti pour voir ce qui se passait. Je me suis dirigé vers le compteur pour couper le courant, mais j’ai compris que c’est à ce niveau que l’incendie s’était déclaré. Je ne pouvais donc pas intervenir sur le compteur », a-t-il expliqué. Poursuivant son témoignage, il a décrit l’ampleur des dégâts tout en saluant la mobilisation des citoyens et l’intervention des sapeurs-pompiers. « Les dégâts sont énormes. La chambre où le feu a commencé a été complètement réduite en cendres, de même que les deux chambres voisines. C’est au salon que nous avons pu sauver quelques affaires, ainsi que dans la quatrième chambre. Nous remercions sincèrement les citoyens qui nous ont porté secours avant même l’arrivée des sapeurs-pompiers. À leur arrivée, ces derniers ont également fait preuve de beaucoup de courage et de professionnalisme », a-t-il ajouté. De son côté, le commandant adjoint de la Protection civile de Labé, Tinguiano Émilie, a expliqué les circonstances de l’intervention de ses équipes. Il a notamment souligné l’importance d’une intervention rapide pour empêcher la propagation des flammes. « C’était un bâtiment d’habitation qui avait pris feu. Heureusement, nous avons été alertés à temps et nous sommes rapidement intervenus. À notre arrivée, nous avons constaté que la population avait déjà commencé à lutter contre les flammes. Nous avons alors essayé de maîtriser le feu afin d’éviter sa propagation. Il n’y a pas eu de blessés et l’intervention s’est bien déroulée », a-t-il indiqué. Concernant l’origine du sinistre, le responsable de la Protection civile a évoqué la piste d’un court-circuit électrique. Il a également précisé que l’intervention avait nécessité l’appui d’un agent d’Électricité de Guinée (EDG). « Pendant l’intervention, nous avons constaté des picotements électriques. Il a donc fallu faire appel à un agent d’EDG pour isoler la maison du réseau électrique. Les dégâts sont importants, puisque deux à trois chambres ont été entièrement consumées par les flammes », a-t-il précisé. Profitant de cette occasion, le commandant adjoint de la Protection civile a lancé un appel à la population de Labé, l’invitant à alerter rapidement les services de secours dès les premiers signes d’incendie et à éviter toute intervention susceptible de mettre des vies en danger. « Je demande à la population de Labé, dès qu’elle constate un début d’incendie, de ne pas chercher à jouer aux pompiers, mais plutôt de nous alerter à temps. Cela nous permettra d’intervenir rapidement. Un autre problème que nous rencontrons sur le terrain concerne les citoyens qui, lorsque nous intervenons, veulent également participer aux opérations et faire comme nous. Nous voulons travailler efficacement, mais surtout éviter qu’il y ait d’autres victimes. Il faut donc qu’ils acceptent de nous laisser travailler », a-t-il lancé. Ce nouvel incendie rappelle l’importance de la prévention des risques électriques et de la collaboration entre les populations et les services de secours pour limiter les dégâts en cas de sinistre. Alpha Moussa Dieng, correspondant régional à Labé L’article Labé : un court-circuit provoque un incendie qui ravage plusieurs chambres à Daka 1 est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: DR Congo: Ebola disease survivors share their stories
items.description: Country: Democratic Republic of the Congo Source: Médecins Sans Frontières Christine and her ten-year-old son, Jérémie, fell sick with Ebola disease after attending a funeral in September. “Soon after getting home, I started to get headaches,” says Christine. “The next day, it got worse.” The pair visited a local hospital, but as their symptoms – vomiting and diarrhoea – got worse, they were eventually transferred to the Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) Ebola treatment centre (ETC) in Beni, North Kivu province, Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) . Medical staff feared they would not make it. In the more than six months since the Ebola disease outbreak was declared in DRC, close to 12,000 people have been infected, according to the Ministry of Health. The true figure is certainly higher. Around half of the people who are infected die from the disease. One of the reasons that the mortality rate is so high is that many people seek care only when the disease has already reached an advanced stage. “We can do more to increase the chances of survival of patients who come as soon as they experience symptoms,” says Dr Louis Vala Moweni, medical coordinator for MSF’s Ebola response. “But many arrive too late.” Ebola disease can progress rapidly and lead to severe complications. This is why patients should seek medical care as soon as they develop early symptoms, such as fever and headaches. Although the outbreak was officially declared in May, many people still hesitate to come to ETCs because of fear, misinformation, and distrust towards the Ebola response. “I thought that no one makes it out of here alive and that doctors and nurses kill people,” says Ghislaine, another survivor recently discharged from the Beni ETC. “I was surprised to experience the opposite.” For Dr Moweni, high levels of fear in the community are understandable. “At the beginning of the outbreak, people saw medical staff arriving in full personal protective equipment (PPE) and taking patients away,” he says. “Regrettably, many people died. We need to acknowledge that this instils fear in communities.” However, thanks to their testimonies, survivors are now helping to counter rumours and strengthen communities’ trust in health teams. “Seeing survivors walk out of ETCs alive, and hearing what they have to say is one of the best ways to combat that fear,” says Dr Moweni. In Mongbwalu, Ituri province, where the outbreak originated, there were significant fears when we began our response in May. “People were dying in cascades,” recalls Deogracias Kasereka, a pastor from the town, who later fell ill after presiding over a funeral. His daughter, who had worked on a previous outbreak, encouraged him to get tested for Ebola disease. “At that time, people were afraid, because going to the hospital meant death,” says Pastor Kasereka. “But I made up my mind. I said to myself, ‘if I must die of Ebola, then I will die. And if I can be cured, then I will be cured’. So, I decided to go.” After testing positive, the pastor was treated at the ETC and, in June, became the first patient in the town to recover from Ebola disease. Patients started to arrive at earlier stages of infection and mortality rates among them began to fall. “When they saw me alive, it encouraged many people,” he says. “They had said, ‘Even the pastor will die’. But seeing me return gave people hope.” “From the day I was discharged, I began awareness-raising in the community,” says Pastor Kasereka. “I went directly into the church communities to speak to people. Since then, I have continued this work, even in schools.” While attitudes towards the response are changing in some areas, some survivors still face acute stigma. “There is often a paradox in the experience of survivors,” says Dr Moweni. “While they want to put their experience to the benefit of their communities and contribute to the fight against the outbreak, they can also become victims of stigma and attacks. This adds to their suffering at a time when they are still recovering from the disease.” When Francine, who fell ill with Ebola disease after losing one of her children to the disease, was discharged from the Mongbwalu ETC in October, she found that the community had burned down her home — fearing it to be contaminated. “I do not want to speak with them anymore,” says Francine. “I do not know how I will survive.” At a survivor clinic supported by MSF, and adjacent to Mongbwalu ETC, patients receive medical and psychological support through individual consultations. MSF pays for transport costs to help survivors living far away reach the clinic. “Some survivors are feared in their communities,” says Jean-Paul Wayotho Pariu, an MSF health promoter. “We advise them how to reintegrate and how to avoid shame and feel at ease. The perception of this disease makes many people see it as shameful.” Despite the challenges, patients who survive Ebola disease also feel great relief. “I am happy to return home,” says Christine, on the day of her release, alongside Jérémie, after more than a month of treatment. “In the ETC, I spent the whole time thinking about my family and my children.” Her message to the community is clear: “If other people feel sick, they should come to the ETC and not stay at home. They [healthcare staff] will look after you.”

items.title: Makkah pact nations to discuss conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis in Islamabad meeting, Asif says
items.description: The Makkah pact nations will discuss the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthi fighters in Yemen when officials from the mutual defence agreement meet in Islamabad on Thursday, Defence Minister Khawaja Asif told AFP . Asif said the “continuous turmoil south of Saudi Arabia will obviously be one agenda point in the meeting and it is very important”, confirming that defence and foreign ministers from the Gulf kingdom, Turkiye and Pakistan would attend. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed the pact in August , with the three Muslim nations pledging to come to each other’s aid in the event of an attack. Saudi Arabia has faced repeated barrages by the Houthis in Yemen, with the group targeting cities, oil facilities and shipping since fighting in Yemen’s civil war intensified in July. “Any threat to Saudi Arabia is a threat to Pakistan and Turkiye according to the pact, which is absolutely clear,” Khawaja said on Wednesday, praising Riyadh’s handling of the conflict with the Houthis, who hold swathes of territory in Yemen, including its capital Sanaa. He said the pact, which was formed during the expansion of the war in the Middle East following US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February , was still at a “nascent stage”. “Initially, we need to have frequent meetings to steer what is being formulated, in a way that in the next couple of months we have everything in place so that we can move forward,” he added. Khawaja declined to comment on how the pact would react to a direct attack by Iran on Saudi Arabia and identified Israel as a possible threat to other countries in the region. “The possibility of some conflict, or aggression from the Israeli side exists, so we need to close our ranks, the countries of this region,” he said. Pakistan brokered a June accord that led to a brief halt in fighting between the US and Iran and set a roadmap for further agreement on reopening the crucial Strait of Hormuz and for negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear programme. But the truce collapsed, with Washington and Tehran accusing each other of violating the agreement, prompting months of shuttle diplomacy to resuscitate the ceasefire, led principally by mediators Qatar and Pakistan. Khawaja said Pakistan had played “a very, very constructive role” between Washington and Tehran, but the outcome of ongoing mediation was “still fragile” and peace was “not yet embedded in a way people were expecting”.

items.title: ‎Médailles du travail : Comilog honore 29 de ses agents pour leur fidélité et leur engagement
items.description: ‎‎À l’occasion des festivités de la Sainte-Barbe, la Compagnie minière de l’Ogooué (Comilog) a récompensé 29 de ses salariés en poste à Owendo, ce jeudi 26 novembre 2026, lors d’une cérémonie de remise de médailles organisée à l’hôtel Boulevard d’Acaé. Une distinction destinée à saluer leur fidélité, leur engagement et les années consacrées au développement de l’entreprise. Photo de famille à l'issue de la cérémonie de remise de médailles, le 26 novembre 2026 à Owendo. © GabonReview La cérémonie de remise de médailles de la Compagnie minière de l’Ogooué (Comilog) s’est tenue jeudi 26 novembre 2026 à l’hôtel Boulevard d’Acaé. À cet effet, 29 salariés en poste à Owendo ont été décorés, à savoir huit médaillés de bronze, vingt d’argent et un seul médaillé d’or, récompensé pour ses 30 années de service au sein de la compagnie. Prenant la parole au nom de la direction générale, le directeur général de la Communication de Comilog, Aunel Loumba, a rappelé que ces distinctions récompensent bien plus que des années de présence au sein de la compagnie. «Ce sont 29 parcours différents, 29 histoires différentes au sein de notre entreprise» , a-t-il souligné, évoquant les transformations organisationnelles, les évolutions des méthodes de travail ainsi que les périodes difficiles traversées par les récipiendaires. Pour lui, ces salariés ont, chacun à leur niveau, contribué à écrire l'histoire de Comilog. ‏La cérémonie a également été l'occasion de rappeler l'importance de la transmission des compétences entre les générations. «Beaucoup de choses s'apprennent à l'école et en formation, mais beaucoup ne s'apprennent que sur le terrain» , a indiqué Aunel Loumba, estimant que l'expérience acquise par les anciens constitue une richesse à partager avec les jeunes collaborateurs et les nouveaux arrivants. ‎ ‎Un appel à transmettre l'expérience aux jeunes collaborateurs Quelques moments de la cérémonie. © GabonReview Dans la même dynamique, le directeur général du Travail, Luc Agondjo, a invité les récipiendaires à poursuivre leur engagement en mettant leur expérience au service des collaborateurs moins anciens. Rappelant les sacrifices consentis durant ces années de carrière, il les a encouragés à s'interroger sur leur contribution future à la compagnie. «Vous avez encore à donner à Comilog. Vous avez à donner votre professionnalisme, votre savoir-faire et votre savoir-être» , a-t-il déclaré, insistant sur la nécessité de préparer la relève afin que les départs futurs ne compromettent ni la continuité des activités ni les performances de l'entreprise. ‎‎Parmi les travailleurs distingués figure Évariste Idongui Ndjiba, récipiendaire de la médaille d'or pour ses 30 années de service au sein de Comilog. Invité à partager le secret de cette longévité professionnelle, il a mis en avant la volonté, l'abnégation et le respect des consignes. «Il n'y a pas de secret : c'est juste la volonté, l'abnégation, le respect de la hiérarchie et surtout des orientations qu'on nous donne. Il faut se donner et respecter les consignes» , a-t-il confié, avant d'encourager les jeunes générations à faire preuve de la même détermination. ‎‎C'est donc une cérémonie qui, au-delà des distinctions individuelles, met en avant la place du capital humain dans la construction et la pérennité de Comilog. ‎Thécia Nyomba L’article ‎Médailles du travail : Comilog honore 29 de ses agents pour leur fidélité et leur engagement est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Security breach case: IHC seeks replies from parties on Imaan, Hadi's appeals against their conviction
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) on Thursday issued notices and sought replies from parties on appeals filed by lawyers Imaan Zainab Hazir-Mazari and Hadi Ali Chattha against their convictions in a security breach case. An anti-terrorism court (ATC) sentenced the husband-wife duo to 10 years in prison each, besides imposing fines on them, on Oct 29 in the 2024 case pertaining to the removal of security barriers, disruption of an international cricket team’s security route and incitement to public unrest. Imaan and Hadi filed appeals in the IHC against their convictions on Nov 7. They also sought the suspension of their sentences and release on bail pending the outcome of their appeals. A division bench comprising Justice Inam Ameen Minhas and Justice Ayaz Shaukat took up their appeals today and issued the notices to the parties through a written order. The court also issued notices and sought responses from parties on separate applications filed by both appellants for the suspension of their sentences. Advocates Riasat Ali Azad, Zainab Janjua and Asif Ali Tamboli represented Imaan and Hadi at the hearing today. Jailed, sentenced, re-arrested They have been in jail since their arrest on Jan 23 in a case registered against them for protesting outside the IHC and allegedly manhandling the IHC Bar Association president. The arrest prompted criticism by rights bodies, politicians and journalists, who stressed the couple’s right to a fair trial. Just a day later, a sessions court sentenced them to 17 years on multiple charges under the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act in the controversial social media posts case. The convictions were widely condemned by lawyers and United Nations (UN) experts . On September 17, following months of litigation before the courts , the SC suspended their sentences in the case. The SC ordered their release pending the IHC’s final verdict on their appeals against the trial court’s decision. However, the reprieve was short-lived as hours later, Islamabad police arrested the couple again in connection with another case and produced them before an ATC, which sent them to jail on judicial remand. The fresh case in which the two were arrested was registered at the federal capital’s Kohsar police station on March 22 last year on the complaint of City Magistrate Ghulam Murtaza Chandio. Imaan and Hadi were accused of chanting anti-government slogans and blocking roads and were nominated by name in the FIR. However, at the time of registration of the case, no section of the Anti-Terrorism Act (ATA) had been added. The FIR included sections 188 (disobedience of an order lawfully promulgated by a public servant), 341 (wrongful restraint), 506 (punishment for criminal intimidation), 353 (assault or use of criminal force to deter a public servant from discharging their official duty) and 186 (obstructing a public servant in the performance of official duties). While they remain imprisoned, their trial in the security breach case was conducted in jail. They were indicted in the case on Oct 7, despite their objections that they had not received copies of case documents and had not been allowed to meet their lawyers. On Oct 26, they had also approached the Supreme Court challenging the IHC’s refusal to stay their jail trial. On Nov 11, the Supreme Court disposed of a petition filed by the couple as infructuous, observing that the matter had become infructuous following the conclusion of the trial and their conviction. The Supreme Court directed the IHC to decide on the petition filed by the couple in the case.

items.title: Solidarité et responsabilité sociale : l’ARSJPA aux côtés des personnes atteintes d’albinisme en Guinée
items.description: L’Autorité de régulation du secteur des jeux et pratiques assimilées (ARSJPA) entend donner une dimension humaine et solidaire à sa mission institutionnelle. À travers une initiative en faveur de l’Union des personnes atteintes d’albinisme de Guinée (UPAAG), l’institution réaffirme son engagement en faveur de la protection des personnes vulnérables et de l’amélioration des conditions de vie des populations. Cette action de solidarité traduit une volonté de faire de la responsabilité sociale un axe concret de l’engagement de l’ARSJPA auprès des communautés. Un soutien concret aux personnes atteintes d’albinisme Au cœur de cette initiative figure le soutien apporté aux personnes atteintes d’albinisme, particulièrement exposées à certains risques sanitaires et aux difficultés liées à leur condition. L’un des gestes importants annoncés est la remise de crèmes solaires, indispensables à la protection de leur peau contre les effets nocifs des rayonnements ultraviolets. Au-delà de ce don, cette démarche contribue à attirer l’attention sur les besoins spécifiques des personnes atteintes d’albinisme et sur la nécessité de renforcer leur accompagnement sanitaire et social. À travers son appui à l’UPAAG, l’ARSJPA entend également contribuer à une meilleure prise en compte de cette catégorie de la population, qui mérite une attention particulière, davantage de protection et une pleine participation à la vie sociale. Une responsabilité sociale qui dépasse le cadre institutionnel L'engagement de l'ARSJPA ne se limite pas à cette seule initiative. La démarche présentée dans sa campagne de communication s'inscrit dans une vision plus large de solidarité, articulée autour de plusieurs priorités : le soutien aux personnes vulnérables, l'accompagnement de la jeunesse, l'assistance aux orphelins et aux malades, ainsi que la promotion de l'accès à l'eau potable. Ces différentes orientations témoignent d'une approche de la responsabilité sociale qui place le bien-être des populations au centre des préoccupations. En soutenant des initiatives à vocation sociale et humanitaire, l'ARSJPA entend ainsi contribuer, à son niveau, aux efforts de solidarité nationale et à la construction d'une société plus inclusive. Une cérémonie officielle sous le signe de la solidarité La cérémonie officielle de remise du don à l'UPAAG est annoncée pour le samedi 28 novembre 2026, à partir de 9 heures, à l'hôtel Noom de Kaloum, à Conakry. Placée sous le haut patronage du président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, cette initiative constitue une occasion de mettre en lumière les actions de solidarité en faveur des personnes atteintes d'albinisme et de rappeler l'importance de l'engagement des institutions dans l'amélioration des conditions de vie des populations. L'ARSJPA, un engagement pour le bien-être des populations À travers cette action, l'ARSJPA entend rappeler que la régulation et les missions institutionnelles peuvent également s'accompagner d'un engagement citoyen et solidaire. Son initiative en faveur de l'UPAAG illustre cette volonté de contribuer à une société où la dignité humaine, l'inclusion et la protection des personnes vulnérables occupent une place essentielle. Un engagement pour la solidarité et le bien-être des populations.
